articles.title: How Grandma’s Thanksgiving Recipes Compare to Popular Packaged Options
articles.content:
For Jennifer Gaily, Thanksgiving meant a 10-course meal her Irish grandmother prepared entirely from scratch. The spread included everything from turnips and sweet potatoes to homemade pumpkin, apple, and pecan pies.

“She would make mashed potatoes just for me. One pot of five pressure-cooked potatoes, whole milk, salt, and an entire stick of butter! I ate the whole thing,” Gaily, who lives in New Jersey, told the Epoch Times.

Families like Gaily’s see Thanksgiving dinner as the quintessential American meal, but the memories surrounding it often begin before everyone gathers around the table—in the kitchen, watching grandma peel potatoes, tear bread for stuffing, simmer cranberries, or roll out pie dough. In the background, there was the clanking of pots and pans, football announcers, and aromas drifting from the kitchen as guests grew hungry.

Certain dishes, and the people who make them, become part of lifetime memories. Some recipes have been family favorites “for the past 100 years,” Nanette Gremillion of Louisiana told The Epoch Times.

Yet somewhere along the way, we went from transforming basic ingredients and classic dishes at home to swapping in prepared foods that require little more than assembly—boxes, cans, and ingredient lists we can’t pronounce, including emulsifiers, preservatives, and additives.

Every year, millions upon millions of deli-prepared entrees, boxed stuffing mixes, jars of gravy, and cans of jellied cranberries are sold during Thanksgiving. Instacart’s analysis of Thanksgiving shopping from 2025 found that one in four orders containing a whole turkey also included boxed stuffing.

Canned cranberry sauce was also more than twice as likely to appear in carts as fresh cranberries. During the first week of November 2025, consumers spent nearly $19.5 million on stuffing mixes, $8.9 million on cranberry sauce, and $13,196,544 on frozen pies, according to retail scanner data from Circana.

Thanksgiving didn’t necessarily stop being homemade—the definition of homemade changed.

What’s lost when Thanksgiving comes out of a box?

Grandma’s Recipes vs. Boxed and Canned Versions

“The gap is widest with boxed stuffing, instant mashed potatoes, and jarred gravy,” Sarah Otto, a nutritionist, told The Epoch Times.

Because these products are designed to last longer on store shelves, they often contain more sodium, flavor enhancers, and additives such as emulsifiers and thickeners than you wouldn’t typically use when cooking at home.

1. Boxed vs. Homemade Stuffing

Boxed stuffing mixes may be convenient but can also be high in sodium.

Making stuffing from scratch doesn’t mean you have to bake your own bread.

“Buy a good loaf from a bakery or use plain bread cubes. Add sautéed onions, celery, butter, sage, and some good stock. It’s simple, and it’s delicious,” Steve DiFillippo, chef and owner of Davio’s Northern Italian Steakhouse, told The Epoch Times.

If you don’t want to start from scratch, “I would instead start with a boxed stuffing mix and add sauteed onions, celery, mushrooms, and extra herbs. Use low-sodium broth and consider replacing some of the mix with whole-grain bread. This is a simple way to boost nutrition,” Wright said.

2. Boxed Dehydrated Potatoes vs. Homemade Mashed Potatoes

Dehydrated potatoes in and of themselves retain many of the nutrients in fresh potatoes, including potassium, although some vitamin C may be lost during processing.

“Plain instant potatoes can be nutritionally comparable to homemade potatoes, with the biggest differences coming from what gets added,” Wright said.

However, the majority of options that line supermarket shelves for Thanksgiving contain a laundry list of flavorings and additives in an attempt to achieve a “homestyle” and “buttery” flavor.

You may want homemade mashed potatoes without adding another task to Thanksgiving Day. DiFillippo suggests peeling and cutting the potatoes the day before and keeping them in cold water in the refrigerator to prevent browning.

“That’s one less thing to worry about. You can even make the mashed potatoes the day before and reheat them with a little warm milk and butter. Just don’t overmix them,” he said.

If you want to go with store-bought, aim for plain and add the flavor yourself. You can also replace some of the butter or cream with milk or plain Greek yogurt for creaminess and additional protein.

3. Canned vs. Homemade Gravy

Canned and jarred gravies typically contain 220 mg to more than 350 mg of sodium per a quarter cup serving, depending on the brand.

You don’t necessarily need to make your own stock to get flavorful homemade gravy. DiFillippo suggests purchasing a good chicken or turkey stock and adding the drippings from your roasted turkey.

“That’s where all the flavor is. Add them to your stock and make a simple gravy,” he said.

4. Canned Cranberry Sauce vs. Fresh Cranberries

“Fresh and unsweetened frozen cranberries provide fiber and beneficial plant compounds, including polyphenols,” Wright said.

5. Store-Bought Pumpkin Pie vs. Homemade Pumpkin Pie

“Both homemade and store-bought pumpkin pies can contain significant amounts of added sugar, saturated fat and calories,” Wright said.

A pie’s nutritional value depends more on its ingredients and the recipe than whether or not it was store-bought or homemade.

How Thanksgiving Cooking Shifted From Scratch to Convenience

The role of convenience foods for turkey day cooking developed over decades.

The shift toward convenience cooking gained traction mid-century, when frozen food went from being considered a luxury reserved for affluent housewives to being more widely advertised as an affordable dinner option. One dish in particular shines a light on this transition.

Green bean casserole was created in 1955 by Dorcas Reilly, a home economist and recipe developer working in Campbell’s Soup Company’s test kitchen in Camden, New Jersey.

“It was invented to be quick and easy—a ‘fancy’ meal that a housewife could make with just the cans and other ingredients she had around the house,” Mike Davis, who holds a doctorate in American history and is an adjunct professor at Lees-McRae College told The Epoch Times.

What began as a practical recipe became a Thanksgiving tradition that still holds roots today. The dish also highlights the ways home cooks embraced convenience foods and made them part of traditions.

“A generation of American women took what Dorcas Reilly gave them and made it their own,” Davis said.

How to Cut Back on Packaged Foods

For some people, like Denise Dixon of California, preparing a homemade meal is an honor and a meaningful expression of love for her precious people.

“I know how much they appreciate the thought and effort that goes into it,” she told The Epoch Times.

But making a memorable Thanksgiving meal doesn’t mean you have to make everything from scratch.

“My rule for Thanksgiving is: Make the important things yourself and be smart about the rest. The holiday should still be enjoyable,” DiFillippo said.

Taking a few shortcuts in the kitchen is perfectly fine if it gives you more time to enjoy the holiday with your family.

“Grandma Rita’s one cheat was Pillsbury rolls. She felt they were just as good at the time,” Gaily said.

A few simple adjustments to your holiday meal can make convenience foods more nutritious, while prepping ahead can take some of the pressure off cooking day.

Add Instead of Subtract

“One of my favorites is to add more vegetables rather than simply taking ingredients away. This improves nutrient density while preserving the flavors and traditions people enjoy, especially around the holidays,” Wright said.

Frozen vegetables are often just as nutritious as fresh and can be more economical.

“Add a simple roasted vegetable dish or a fermented side like sauerkraut to bring fiber and variety to a meal that’s mostly starch,” Otto said.

What to Look for on Food Labels

If you are going with store-bought, Chad Larson, a naturopathic physician, recommends scanning labels for sodium, added sugar, saturated fat, and fiber.

“Compare the amounts of the same serving size shown on the packages. See how to prepare the food, since added liquids, fats, and solids can make a big difference in the nutritional value,” Larson said.

“Look at the whole plate,” Otto said. “How much fiber, how many vegetables, and how much sodium and added sugar across the meal—rather than treating any single dish as good or bad.”

Thanksgiving comes just once a year—the extra effort to make it special is worth it.

articles.title: Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Shield Camera and Microphone Data
articles.content:
Apple has published a detailed description of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture in its silicon designed to keep camera and microphone data used for ambient sensing isolated from the main operating system.

Ambient sensing lets a device listen for “Hey Siri”. On the recently introduced HomeView smart display, it enables the recognition of user faces and voices.

Secure Exclaves are isolated runtimes that handle camera and microphone data apart from the rest of the device.

“Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple,” the company said.

The design is built around three requirements. The main OS must not be able to pull out or alter data handled in an exclave, and only a narrowly defined set of information may cross over to it. Users must also be able to tell when a sensor session is active, without the main OS interfering.

According to Apple, in background sensing only specific metadata reaches the rest of the system. On HomeView, the recognition result sent to the main OS is a person identifier, position and confidence level, without audio or video data being shared.

When an app requests full sensor access, a dedicated exclave acts as gatekeeper. Sensor data is released only once it has confirmed the indicator is on and has been showing for a sufficient period.

On devices such as the iPhone, where the indicator is an on-screen dot, another exclave checks which pixels were actually drawn to the display.

Apple said Secure Exclaves protect person recognition on HomeView, along with Siri Recap and Live Rewind. They also protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView.

The exclaves run on a minimal, capability-based microkernel, to which Apple has been applying formal verification. Apple said this turned up hard-to-spot but critical flaws in many kernel subsystems that could have led to full kernel compromise. Many of these issues were caught early in development.

The microkernel is still under active development and changes often, Apple noted. “Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts,” it said.

articles.title: No Signs of Hacking in FAA Ground Stop as FBI Reportedly Probes Software Update
articles.content:
US officials have found no evidence that hackers caused the outage that led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt flight departures nationwide on Friday, and the FBI is reportedly examining whether a software update was responsible.

The FAA issued the ground stop on November 13 after a communications problem hit its air route traffic control centers. The order was lifted at 8:15 pm ET, more than four hours later, after disrupting thousands of flights. Departures have since resumed, though officials expect delays to continue for several days.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the incident did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack, and that the failure appeared to be mechanical.

On the absence of attack indicators, Mullin said “there’s no chatter, we haven’t seen any footprints.”

He stopped short of dismissing the possibility entirely. “However, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out,” Mullin said.

The NSA, the Department of Defense, CISA and other agencies have been involved in the investigation, according to Mullin.

The FBI does not think a cyberattack or criminal activity was behind the outage, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Investigators are looking at a software update as a potential cause, the source said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed legacy equipment. He said switches and routers in the FAA’s network were flooded with data and began producing inconsistent information, at which point the agency shut the system down.

Officials described the ground stop as a precaution.

Mullin offered a possible trigger. He said it appeared the FAA had been applying patches and installing new equipment and technology, which “was overwhelming the older system.”

CBS News, citing multiple sources, reported that the outage followed an update to the private communications network that links the air traffic control system. The network rebooted and then crashed, and it is operated by L3Harris, according to the report.

Officials said the incident had nothing to do with the Microsoft outage earlier in the week. They also said the FAA’s recently deployed AI systems played no role.

No official root cause has been announced.

The previous nationwide ground stop came in January 2023, after a contractor unintentionally deleted files while working on the system that delivers safety notices to pilots. No evidence of a cyberattack was found in that case either.

articles.title: Laba-Laba yang Sangat Cerdas
articles.content:
Sumber: www.creationmoments.com

Selama lebih dari satu abad, para ilmuwan telah bertanya-tanya mengenai hiasan-hiasan yang ditenun oleh setidaknya 78 spesies laba-laba ke dalam jaring mereka. Tambahan berupa garis-garis dan pola berbentuk huruf ‘X’ tersebut tampak tidak memiliki tujuan yang jelas. Beberapa pihak menduga bahwa pola-pola itu mungkin berfungsi sebagai tempat persembunyian, pelindung dari sinar matahari, peringatan bagi burung, atau umpan untuk serangga. Kini, seorang peneliti di Universitas Kyoto mungkin telah menemukan tujuan dari desain-desain tersebut. Jika dugaannya benar, teori evolusi bisa jadi justru ‘terjerat’ oleh jaring laba-laba ini.

Laba-laba Asia yang diteliti oleh peneliti tersebut mampu membuat dua jenis jaring yang berbeda. Saat kenyang, laba-laba ini menambahkan pita-pita sutra di sepanjang jari-jari jaringnya. Namun, saat lapar, ia mengatur pita-pita tersebut hingga membentuk pola spiral yang mengarah ke pusat jaring. Setelah menguji tingkat ketegangan pada kedua jenis jaring tersebut, ia menemukan bahwa jaring dengan pola spiral jauh lebih sensitif — bahkan terhadap serangga terkecil sekalipun — dibandingkan dengan jaring yang hanya memiliki pita-pita biasa. Dengan kata lain, laba-laba yang lapar sedang mencari serangga apa pun yang bisa dimangsa, sementara laba-laba yang kenyang hanya tertarik pada serangga yang lebih besar. Pertanyaannya, bagaimana mungkin evolusi yang tidak berakal dapat memberikan pengetahuan tentang rekayasa struktural yang diperlukan untuk menciptakan desain-desain ini kepada laba-laba? Terlebih lagi, menurut pohon evolusi laba-laba, pengetahuan ini harusnya telah berevolusi setidaknya sembilan kali! Penjelasan yang jauh lebih logis dan lugas adalah bahwa Sang Pencipta memberikan pengetahuan ini kepada laba-laba saat Ia menciptakan mereka.” Ref: Science News, ‘Hungry spiders tune up web jiggliness.’”

articles.title: Kesaksian Seorang Wanita Kristen tentang Cara Berpakaian
articles.content:
Sumber: www.wayoflife.org

Saya sungguh ingin berterima kasih karena Anda telah menulis buku Dressing for the Lord (Berpakaian bagi Tuhan). Buku ini sangat membantu dalam pendalaman Alkitab saya, sehingga saya sampai pada kesimpulan mengenai cara berpakaian. Melalui hal ini, Tuhan benar-benar telah mengubah hati saya dan membuat saya rendah hati. … Hal yang sungguh menyadarkan saya akan kebenaran terjadi saat saya sedang dalam masa pendalaman tersebut. Saya melihat dua pria — di toko yang sama namun pada hari yang berbeda saat saya sedang berbelanja — yang berpakaian dan bertingkah laku layaknya wanita. … sejujurnya, reaksi pertama dalam hati saya adalah rasa jijik dan tersinggung sebagai seorang wanita. Pria-pria ini benar-benar mengolok-olok makna menjadi seorang wanita. Mereka juga membuang jati diri pria yang luar biasa, yang telah dirancang oleh Tuhan bagi mereka. Hal ini membuat saya merasa jijik sekaligus sedih.

Saat menceritakan kejadian ini kepada beberapa teman dan menjelaskan perasaan saya, tiba-tiba terlontar pertanyaan: mungkinkah seperti inilah perasaan kaum pria dahulu, ketika wanita mulai mengenakan celana panjang? Saya pun terdiam dan menyadari bahwa Tuhan baru saja menegur saya melalui perkataan saya sendiri. Pada hari itulah saya memutuskan untuk menyingkirkan celana panjang saya, melakukan perubahan besar, membiarkan rambut saya tumbuh panjang, dan terus membiarkannya tetap panjang. Selain itu, di Irlandia, kami baru saja menyaksikan kaum feminis kembali menang telak dalam pemungutan suara untuk melegalkan aborsi di negara ini. Gerakan feminis ini adalah kelompok yang sama dengan pihak yang memelopori penggunaan celana panjang bagi wanita, yang secara vokal dan gencar mendorong paham androgini serta homoseksualitas. Mereka bahkan berpawai di Washington DC dengan mengenakan pakaian yang vulgar dan menjijikkan demi memperjuangkan aborsi, dan kini mereka terus mendorong praktik aborsi di seluruh dunia.

Jika orang-orang yang mendukung pembunuhan massal terhadap anak-anak tak berdosa—serta memicu kebingungan gender dan merusak rancangan Tuhan — adalah kelompok yang sama dengan pihak yang memulai tren memotong rambut wanita menjadi pendek dan mengenakan celana panjang, maka saya ingin menegaskan kepada siapa pun yang melihat saya bahwa saya sama sekali tidak terlibat dalam kejahatan ini.

Setelah memutuskan untuk berhenti mengenakan celana panjang, Tuhan menunjukkan kepada saya bahwa kesantunan dalam berpakaian — dengan mengenakan busana layaknya seorang wanita — berkaitan dengan sesuatu yang jauh lebih dalam di dalam hati. Hal ini merupakan simbol kerendahan hati. Ini tentang belajar untuk memiliki roh yang lemah lembut dan tenang. Ini tentang mengakui serta menghormati otoritas yang ditetapkan Tuhan dalam hidup kita, dan merasa puas menjadi sosok sebagaimana Tuhan menciptakan kita — yang merupakan jati diri terbaik bagi kita. Saat saya mengenakan rok panjang yang longgar dan menutup bagian tubuh yang memang seharusnya tertutup, saya sedang dengan rendah hati tunduk kepada Tuhan dan kepada otoritas yang telah Ia tetapkan dalam hidup saya. Saya telah belajar bahwa dalam ketundukan tersebut, saya terlindungi, baik secara rohani maupun jasmani.

articles.title: Kristus Palsu Versi Kid Rock
articles.content:
Sumber: www.wayoflife.org

“Tetapi aku takut, jangan-jangan sebagaimana sang ular telah menipu Hawa dengan kelicikannya, demikian juga pikiran kalian telah diselewengkan dari kesederhanaan yang ada dalam Kristus. 4 Sebab jika seseorang datang memberitakan Yesus yang lain, yang tidak pernah kami beritakan, atau jika kalian mendapatkan roh yang lain, yang tidak kalian terima sebelumnya, atau injil yang lain yang tidak kalian sambut sebelumnya, kalian begitu sabar membiarkannya” (2 Korintus 11:3-4).

Kid Rock (nama aslinya Robert Ritchie) — yang begitu membanggakan musik rock & roll yang kotor hingga ia menjadikannya sebagai nama panggungnya — memiliki album baru berjudul Halfway 2 Jesus. Rapper yang tercela, Eminem, turut tampil sebagai bintang tamu. (Kid Rock dikenal luas karena gaya hidupnya yang penuh pesta pora, perzinaan, kekerasan, kata-kata kasar, serta penyalahgunaan narkoba dan alkohol; ia mendukung aborsi, pernikahan sesama jenis, dan legalisasi narkoba. Album-album sebelumnya antara lain Devil Without a Cause, Cocky, Rebel Soul, Early Mornin’ Stoned Pimp, dan Bad Reputation.)

Dalam sebuah wawancara baru-baru ini dengan Lara, menantu Presiden Trump, Kid Rock menjelaskan kekristenannya sebagai berikut: “Setelah Charlie Kirk dibunuh, seperti banyak orang lainnya, saya mulai merasa lebih dekat dengan iman saya. Jadi, saya mulai menulis lagu-lagu ini, dan tiba-tiba saja lagu-lagu itu datang begitu saja kepada saya. Saya paham mengapa ada skeptisisme. Orang-orang bertanya, ‘Apakah Kid Rock sudah diselamatkan?’ Maksud saya, saya tidak ‘diselamatkan.’ Saya tetaplah Kid Rock. Saya masih akan minum bir dan mengisap cerutu. Saya merasa selama ini hubungan saya dengan Tuhan sudah baik-baik saja.”

Perhatikan bahwa Kid Rock secara terus terang menyatakan bahwa ia tidak mengalami keselamatan dan tidak mengubah gaya hidupnya. Ia mengeklaim bahwa hubungannya dengan Tuhan selalu baik, yang berarti ia tidak pernah mengalami pertobatan — tidak pernah beralih dari kematian menuju kehidupan, atau dari kegelapan menuju terang. Alkitab menyatakan, “Jadi jika seseorang berada dalam Kristus, ia adalah ciptaan baru, hal-hal lama sudah berlalu, sesungguhnya segala sesuatu telah menjadi baru” (2 Kor. 5:17). Alkitab juga mengatakan, “Mereka mengaku mengenal Allah, tetapi mereka memungkiri Dia melalui pekerjaan-pekerjaan mereka, karena mereka keji dan durhaka dan terbukti gagal dalam setiap hal yang baik” (Titus 1:16).

Yesus versi Kid Rock adalah Kristus palsu yang — berbeda dengan Kristus dalam Kitab Suci — tidak menyerukan pertobatan (Luk. 3:1-5) maupun kelahiran baru (Yoh. 3:1-8). Ia tidak menuntut penyangkalan diri (Mat. 16:24), serta tidak memberikan peringatan mengenai api neraka yang kekal (Mat. 5:22; 7:19; 13:40, 42, 50; 18:8, 9; 25:41), iblis (Yoh. 8:44), pengajar palsu (Mat. 7:15-20), ataupun kekristenan palsu (Mat. 7:21-23). ??Yesus versi Kid Rock adalah Yesus ala pop Amerika, Yesus versi Fox News, atau Yesus versi politik konservatif yang menerima segala hal yang berlabel “Kristen”: sakramentalisme, baptisan bayi, keselamatan sebagai sebuah proses, kekristenan yang mendukung homoseksualitas, kepausan, adorasi hosti, venerasi kepada orang kudus, doa kepada Maria, fenomena dibunuh dalam Roh, praktik “bahasa roh” yang tidak dapat dipahami, pendeta perempuan, serta gaya hidup yang menuruti hawa nafsu pribadi.

articles.title: The firewall becomes the foothold: Attackers turn Check Point gateways against customers
articles.content:
Attackers chained a newly disclosed privilege escalation vulnerability with PHP2Shell to take control of gateways, steal network configurations and deploy destructive malware.

A firewall is intended to be a boundary attackers can’t cross.

But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. The patches address a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039, that gives attackers root privilege access and the ability to send commands to the Gaia OS Dynamic CLI daemon, a core background process.

Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted.

Perhaps not surprisingly, adversaries gained initial access via PHP2Shell, the collective name for two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The 9.2-severity-rated bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

“For customers, one foothold delivered the full menu: Spying, staying, and destroying,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “For Check Point, the cost is trust. A firewall is supposed to be the strongest point in the network, not the softest.”

Granting unintended root access

CVE-2026-123039 is a bug in the Dynamic CLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface which sends privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS Dynamic CLI. It is a local privilege escalation flaw, meaning an attacker already has to have local code execution ability on the appliance; this accounts for its 7.8 rating.

Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. They then escalated privileges to root using the CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

“Once attackers have root, they can run anything they like,” Dickson said. A management service on the appliance runs as root, listens on a local socket that any process on the box can write to, and never checks who is calling.

In this case, the attackers hid web shells inside the templates the portal uses to build its login page, and installed a TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that survives reboots, tucks itself into backups and snapshots, and hides inside the appliance’s own processes, he explained.

“That backdoor can copy the firewall configuration, which is essentially a blueprint of the network,” he said. It can also alter the firewall’s logs, concealing the attacker’s activities.

Check Point reported that, after gaining root access, the attackers then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed messages signed by a group calling itself Dream Security Ltd during the destructive stage.

Check Point advised security teams to immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes, beginning with devices that expose Mobile Access to the internet. Those who can’t do so right away should stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. However, they warned, this can come at the cost of some CLI commands.

Dickson also advised customers to turn off Mobile Access where it is not used, keep management interfaces off the internet entirely, and run the advisory’s log checks on any gateway exposed since late October, then cut the cord between the firewall and the hypervisor. A potentially exposed gateway should never have a trusted path into VMware ESXi.

They should also ship firewall logs off the box, as they happen, to a system the firewall cannot touch.

Products impacted by CVE-2026-123039 include Check Point’s Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms.

Security tools are as big a target as what they protect

Once attackers have root access, the device basically becomes a trusted launching point for attacks against other systems that would otherwise stay protected, explained Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. By effectively controlling the gateway, they can execute a wide array of nefarious actions.

The overall takeaway and irony of this, Avakian pointed out, is that the very technology organizations deploy to protect themselves can become one of their greatest vulnerabilities.

“Organizations can no longer assume their security infrastructure is inherently secure simply because it’s designed to provide protection,” he said. In reality, it is as much of a target as the systems it’s protecting.

Firewalls, VPN appliances, and security gateways are increasingly being targeted because they provide the greatest leverage and control, he noted. As such, security teams must treat these appliances as high value assets with the same access control safeguards, vulnerability management, monitoring, and incident response rigor applied to other critical infrastructure.

This means aggressively patching internet facing systems, restricting management access, monitoring for unusual administrative activity, and looking for indications of persistence or lateral movement, he said. But patches don’t evict already established attackers, so security teams must investigate and, where necessary, rebuild affected systems from trusted images.

And with AI accelerating attacks, CISOs should consider establishing a zero trust mindset and architecture collectively across the pillars of identity, network, applications, data, and devices, he said.

Keep an eye on the edge

Edge devices are primary targets, as they sit at the boundary, hold privileged access, and rarely get the endpoint monitoring that other systems do, noted Scott Miserendino, CTO at DataBee. Security appliances should be treated as the high-risk assets they’ve become.

In addition to patching and applying mitigations, he advised, defenders should assume there’s been a breach, hunting for published indicators of compromise (IOCs), routinely investigating network and endpoint security logs, and segmenting networks to reduce blast radius. “Security tools aren’t automatically secure, so defend the defenders,” he said.

And, Dickson pointed out, PHP2Shell will keep showing up because PHP sits underneath so much web software, including the portals bolted onto security appliances, so it should always be on defenders’ radar.

The management plane is a key target

Check Point is not alone as a victim of threat actors. Firewall management has become a favorite target for attackers across the industry.

In January, for instance, Fortinet disclosed that attackers abused its FortiCloud single sign-on to log into other customers’ FortiGate and FortiManager devices and create administrator accounts. In July and September, CISA added Check Point management server flaws to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities.

That same month, the agency also added a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center flaw, rated a perfect 10.0 in severity, that hands an unauthenticated attacker root access. And, in October, Palo Alto Networks warned of attacks on the PAN-OS management interface, again with “root on the firewall as the prize.”

“The logic is simple,” Dickson said: “The management plane holds the rulebook for the entire network.

Changing providers to one with fewer flaws is an option, but swapping vendors swaps one Achilles’ heel for another, he pointed out, as every vendor’s edge device has a web portal, and every web portal is a door. “The remedy is fewer doors,” he advised. “Shrink the internet-facing edge and put remote access behind one consistent identity policy.”

Ultimately, he noted, a firewall is not a wall, it is a computer sitting on the internet. “Attackers are treating it like one,” he said. “Security teams should defend it like one.”

articles.title: Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
articles.content:
Every repository and organization secret wrapped up in a JSON dump, including credential files from well-known paths, shell histories, and API keys for AI services.

Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials.

Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them.

However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools.

The payload was delivered using at least three methods: modification of existing GitHub Actions workflows, adding a 

postinstall
hook in the 
package.json
file that runs it on any 
npm install
and creating a throw-away branch with a rogue Actions workflow to be run.

“We’ve identified indications that the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories, but this number may understate impact,” the Aikido researchers said in their report. “The run log was deleted in impacted repositories, meaning the threat actor has likely collected the credentials and covered its tracks.”

The npm hook that slipped past GitHub

GitHub’s safeguard against this kind of attack worked as designed for the payloads it could see. The platform has blunted recent workflow-injection campaigns by requiring explicit approval before the malicious workflows run, and GitGuardian found that all seven of the November payload runs still visible in workflow files sat in an 

action_required
state and never started.

“GitHub held the workflow forms, but an npm hook slipped past the hold and ran,” Gaetan Ferry, a security researcher at GitGuardian, said in an analysis.

That’s because the npm hook did not change any workflow file. Instead, the attacker added a hidden script to the repository root and a single line in 

package.json
, which runs on every 
npm install
. The repository’s own unchanged workflows executed 
npm install
as routine build hygiene.

By Thursday the attacker had also changed their exfiltration method. The latest payload sends stolen data only to a Telegram chat, with the HTTP callback now pointing to a dead address. Blocking the previously published IP addresses no longer stops the latest versions.

What the malware steals

Once the script runs, it receives every repository and organization secret through a JSON dump of the workflow’s secrets object. It scans the memory of the runner process, which holds secrets in decrypted form, including ones the workflow never referenced, and collects credential files from well-known paths, shell histories, and API keys for AI services and developer tools such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Copilot, and Cursor.

The script goes further and exchanges OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, mints new long-lived AWS access keys, impersonates GCP service accounts, and replays cached Azure refresh tokens to reach Microsoft Graph and Key Vault.

It packs everything it collects into a gzipped archive and sends it to the attacker then it cleans up. In most repositories the attacker reverted the malicious commit within a minute and deleted the workflow run and its logs.

Backdoors that survive credential rotation

The script also takes actions for attackers to maintain access even if credentials are reset. For AWS it rewrites the assumed role’s trust policy to accept any AWS account, opening the role to anyone, and calls the 

iam:CreateAccessKey
API to create long-lived keys for IAM users.

On Azure it injects federated identity credentials named 

wfx-ci-*
into applications, pointing them back at the compromised repository, so that any workflow in that repository can authenticate to Azure without a stored secret even after every token has been rotated.

If a probe pull request or any of the campaign’s commit strings appear in a repository you control, assume every secret that repository’s workflows could reach is stolen. Rotate repository and organization secrets, package registry tokens, and any cloud keys, and remember that the memory scan means the list of what was taken is wider than what the workflows referenced.

Then hunt for signs of the persistent mechanisms: AWS role trust policies that accept any account, IAM keys created since Nov. 10, and Azure federated credentials named 

wfx-ci-*
.

“Ensure all logs are enabled, particularly audit logs on cloud admin behavior,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “Inspect audit logs where possible (specifically in AWS and Azure, as persistence is possible) to ensure the malicious payload did not run.”

The 

wfx-loot
payload also shipped in published packages: the Packagist package neuronai-studio 3.14.3, and the Go modules docker-env and gocurl. In the Go modules the payload sits only in a workflow file that Go tooling never runs, so consumers may not have been affected; machines that installed the Packagist version should be treated as compromised.

About a fifth of the GitHub accounts used to launch this campaign had already been compromised during the GhostAction attack back in October, GitGuardian said. Meanwhile researchers from StepSecurity traced 173 of the probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub App.

Fly.io confirmed that these tokens were leaked when its deploy process left them in 

.git/config
files inside build directories that some apps served publicly, but noted that Fly.io itself was not breached. GitHub’s bulk revocation of the Fly.io app tokens stopped partway, so some of the stolen token pool may still be valid.

articles.title: FAA Ground Stop Issued Due to ‘Extraordinary Circumstances’
articles.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports on Friday afternoon, citing “extraordinary circumstances” for safety.

According to Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation, the issue stems from communication issue impacting “all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” nationwide.
“The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Duffy posted to X Friday afternoon. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

Was the FAA hit by a cyberattack?

The cause of the air traffic control communications disruption remains unclear. Federal officials have yet to publicly identify what triggered the problem, and it is unclear if the incident is linked to a cyberattack.

The FAA directed departing flights to remain on the ground until further notice and said it would handle inbound international flights case by case. The agency had already halted traffic in Chicago over air traffic control communications problems before issuing the nationwide order.

UPDATE: US officials found no evidence of hacking in the FAA outage that halted flights nationwide, as the FBI reportedly probes an update.

articles.title: The Essential Care That Most Dying People Don’t Get
articles.content:
Lacey already had two tubes coming out of his body. The stent would have to be replaced every few months, and his wife, Thereza Cononi wasn’t sure he had that long to live.

That night, Lacey developed a fever. By the next day, he was back in the hospital. He was sleeping more and eating less, while doctors treated one problem after another.

When Cononi asked for a meeting with those caring for him, the hospital team told her to speak with his oncologist. That appointment wasn’t until May 12.

“He’s not going to be alive on May 12,” she told them.

Lacey’s 33 days in hospice are more than most patients get. Nearly one in three Medicare hospice patients enroll during their final week, according to the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission ​​(MedPAC). One in six enroll in the last three days, some with only hours left.

Some patients decline too quickly to consider hospice. For others, the weeks slip away, packed with appointments and procedures. Families wait for the doctor to say the word. Doctors, unsure how much time remains or reluctant to take away hope, hesitate to bring it up. Patients like Lacey, who’ve survived one crisis after another, hold out for the next treatment.

The question is how to stop the machinery of medicine long enough to ask: Is this next treatment buying more time, or just taking the time that’s left?

What Time in Hospice Buys

By the time Cononi stopped the nurse in the hallway, Lacey was already eligible for hospice. The threshold is a doctor’s judgment that a patient is likely to die within six months. He would live less than three. But no doctor brought it up.

Medicare covers hospice once a patient’s own doctor and a hospice doctor both sign off on that prognosis. It pays hospice a flat daily rate, about $191 per person on average in 2024. That payment must cover all the care the illness requires, from nursing and social work visits to bathing and grooming, as well as medications and any procedure done for comfort. If a hospice spends more than that, it absorbs the difference.

Jason McAvoy, a Massachusetts nurse who has worked in hospice for more than two decades, has seen what time does when a patient arrives at a hospice residence. Accustomed to waiting for help in the hospital, some ring their call bell an hour before they need to use the bathroom, just to be sure someone will come.

“We’re coming when you need something,” he tells them. “When you’re in pain, we’re treating you.” It sometimes takes a while for them to believe it. That trust doesn’t form in a day or two.

Families need something else. “It’s really the preparation,” McAvoy said.

That’s the value of hospice. Throughout the dying process, as changes come, families have someone they know to turn to for support. Hospice also provides the gift of quality time. Instead of sitting in a waiting room, patients and families can be together to say what needs saying and settle what’s unfinished. When a patient arrives with a day or two left, the staff gets the immediate crisis under control, “and that’s pretty much it,” McAvoy said.

Families’ own ratings bear this out. In a 2017

studyin the Journal of Clinical Oncology, families of cancer patients who had more than 30 days in hospice were more likely to call their end-of-life care excellent than families whose loved one had three days or fewer. Families were also more likely to report that their loved ones’ wishes had been followed.

studyof more than 100,000 bereaved family members, Dr. Joan Teno, a physician and adjunct professor at the Brown University School of Public Health, found that what predicted unmet needs and lower satisfaction was not how long hospice lasted, but whether the family felt it had come too late.

Who Says It’s Time?

For hospice to begin, someone has to say it’s time. In Lacey’s case, no one said it explicitly. He didn’t seem ready to hear it, and Cononi learned what it cost her to bring it up. His doctors kept treating.

It ran into April. On April 7, this year, two weeks after the urology appointment, he was preparing for another round of chemotherapy. He had been in and out of the hospital, and Cononi could see him growing weaker by the day.

“Can you please not do chemo today?” she asked.

“No, I’m not giving up,” he told her. “If I don’t get chemo, I don’t have a chance.”

McAvoy has watched that standoff play out in families for two decades. “The family is always trying to protect the patient, and the patient is always trying to protect the family,” he said. “But in my experience, deep down the patient always knows how bad it is.”

Still, Lacey’s hope was understandable. About six months earlier, after a bleed sent him by helicopter to a Boston hospital, doctors told him they were running out of options. The word hospice was briefly mentioned. But Lacey survived another risky procedure. Within weeks, chemo was back up for discussion.

She wanted his doctors to explain what another treatment could realistically accomplish. They discussed his condition with her privately, she said, but rarely brought those conversations into his room.

“Every time I brought them up, I was the bad guy,” she said. She came to believe that his doctors didn’t want to be the ones to tell a man who had repeatedly beaten the odds that his luck had run out.

“If you’ve got a hammer, everything becomes a nail,” McAvoy said. “If you’re a surgeon, you do surgery, even if it’s one in a million.”

Hospice can feel like admitting failure to physicians, rather than offering patients a different kind of care, he said.

Hospice providers interviewed by MedPAC described a similar pattern. Timely referrals were less likely to come from specialists such as oncologists, who often stayed focused on treating the disease until close to the end.

Hospice researcher Megan Mullins, who studies end-of-life care at UT Southwestern Medical Center, described another force at work: treatment momentum. Once treatment begins, it can be difficult to stop.

“One thing fails, we just move automatically on to the next one,” she told The Epoch Times. Rather than reconsidering another round of chemotherapy, doctors may offer it and then “stick the hospice on at the end.”

“They should have been more transparent,” she said, “about what the outcome of the chemo was going to be.”

12 Days Home

In the eight weeks before Lacey entered hospice, Cononi counted just 12 days that he was home. Instead, he spent his days in waiting rooms and hospital beds. In April alone, he went to the emergency room four times.

On his last two hospital admissions, he was under isolation precautions. He couldn’t leave his room, and everyone who came in had to wear a protective gown.

Cancer patients are especially likely to spend their weeks this way, missing out on the benefits of hospice. A 2025 study looked at how more than 315,000 older Americans with cancer spent their last month of life. The ones still getting chemotherapy or other cancer drugs were far more likely to end up in the emergency room, and far less likely to be on hospice, than those who weren’t.

On April 30, two days after being discharged, Lacey woke up to blood in one of his drains. He refused another ambulance ride, so Cononi drove him to the clinic for an outpatient tube check, followed by an antibiotic infusion.

He could barely keep his eyes open. Staff were preparing to send him home when Cononi asked they check his blood pressure. It was 83/47, low enough that his organs were at risk.

Cononi pleaded for someone to admit him. She couldn’t take him home, and the unit couldn’t keep him. The staff called a code, summoning the hospital’s emergency team to take him to the emergency department.

Lacey never went home again.

On May 5, his oncology team finally told him chemotherapy was no longer helping. “It’s harming,” Cononi recalled the oncologist saying.

By then, he was so weak that staff worried he might not survive the 15-minute ambulance transfer to hospice.

33 Days on Hospice

Hospice didn’t change the fact that Lacey was dying. It changed how he spent his remaining days, and how much of his care Cononi had to carry alone.

As he was being admitted, she explained to his nurse why he needed a particular dose of a drug he took for complications of his liver disease. Other providers had challenged the dose. This nurse simply listened. “That’s fine,” the nurse said.

“I didn’t have to fight for him anymore,” she said.

On May 8, a mere three days after arriving at the Respite House, she arrived to find Lacey sitting up, eating breakfast, drinking coffee, and visiting with a friend.

“Oh my God, you’re sitting here. You’re up,” she remembered saying.

Lacey could now choose where to eat. He could go outside to breathe fresh air. He could visit with his dogs. People could visit without gowns or protective equipment.

Friends who were uneasy in a hospital came and stayed. His door went from “being a revolving medical door to a revolving door of happiness, connection, and love.” He stopped being a “pin cushion” and went back to being a husband, an electrician, a friend, a dog father.

“And he got better,” Cononi said.

Not better from his cancer. But better able to enjoy his days. Patients often regain energy when treatments stop, and their symptoms are managed, McAvoy said.

There isn’t much evidence. A 2007 study of 4,500 Medicare patients found that those who had hospice care lived an average of eight days longer than those who did not, a difference that rose to 29 days after accounting for differences between the groups. But the study couldn’t determine whether hospice itself was responsible.

No modern randomized trial has determined if longer life is a benefit of hospice. Such a study would require dying patients to leave a deeply personal choice to change. Living longer, after all, is not what hospice promises.

It promises comfort, and even that is not always straightforward. As fluid built up in Lacey’s abdomen as a result of his cancer, Cononi pushed for a procedure to drain it so he could be more comfortable. Staff initially resisted. McAvoy agreed that draining abdominal fluid can be a comfort measure, though he noted that the high cost can also influence hospice decisions.

Eventually, a physician came to evaluate Lacey. After reviewing his history of severe bleeding, he warned that the procedure could kill him.

“It’s too nice of a day to die,” Lacey said. “I don’t want to die on a sunny day.” He decided against the procedure and lived another two and a half weeks.

There were moments that Lacey struggled with what hospice meant. He asked what would happen if he started bleeding again, and was surprised to hear he wouldn’t return to the hospital. “So they’ll just let me bleed?” he asked.

Cononi and the team reassured him that they would keep him comfortable. The transition was not always easy. But for 33 days, Lacey had time with the people he loved, feeling like a human again, instead of a patient.

He died on June 7.

When to Ask

“The patient has to be ready,” she told The Epoch Times.

But being ready for hospice and being ready to ask a question are different things. Families can ask if the next treatment will benefit the patient long before anyone says hospice. This could help to slow the medical momentum that often keeps people going in treatment.

They also don’t need to wait for a crisis to begin the conversation. Teno recommends consulting palliative medicine or geriatrics as serious illnesses progress to clarify treatment goals and recognize when it might be time for hospice.

Mullins, the hospice researcher, advises families to watch for repeated hospitalizations and changes in everyday functioning. If a patient who once recovered quickly now needs help walking, eating, or managing other ordinary activities, it might be time to consider hospice.

Before agreeing to another treatment, she suggests asking what it will realistically accomplish.

“What can I expect if the illness gets worse?” she said.

McAvoy suggests asking for the estimated chance that a proposed treatment will work, along with what it will demand of the patient’s time and energy.

It’s best to have these discussions before a medical crisis hits, Mullins said. She urges families to talk about what matters most to the patient, including with anyone designated to make decisions on their behalf.

Cononi has thought a lot about the months leading up to Lacey’s death.

“In hindsight, I wish he had gone on hospice care in March,” she said. But she knows he had to come to that decision on his own.

During the 33 days at the hospice residence, something changed for Cononi, too. For six years, she had been his nurse and his advocate. At the Respite House, she got to stop.

“I finally was able to be his wife again,” she said.

articles.title: Vaccine injury patients face uneven access to treatment
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | RSS

Americans who believe they were injured by a vaccine deserve something better than a political argument. They deserve doctors willing to listen, investigate, and help them find a path forward. Too many are still searching for answers while the rest of the country moves on.

The loudest claims have not always helped. Suggesting that everyone who received a COVID vaccine would die or develop myocarditis clouded the issue for people suffering real harm. There are beneficial vaccines. There are also adverse reactions. Recognizing both should not be controversial.

We accept that prescription medicines can cause side effects. Patients report symptoms, physicians weigh the evidence, and treatment changes when necessary. Why should a suspected reaction after an injection be treated as an impossible question?

Dr. Irene Mavrakakis, who describes years of illness following a vaccination in 2012, is trying to turn that question into organized research. Through Liberty Speaks, she is helping assemble a voluntary consortium of physicians and allied health professionals to study potential treatments for vaccine injuries.

Her central point is plain: Scattered treatment experiences are not enough. Physicians need clinical trials, published findings, and a way to share what they learn.

The proposed research includes plasma filtration approaches, stem cells, and other treatment protocols. These are proposals to investigate, not established cures. Independent ethical review and informed consent belong at the beginning of that work.

Mavrakakis says initial fundraising will support institutional review board applications, opening a route toward larger grants and multicenter studies.

That is a practical place to start. Private physicians and concerned citizens do not have to wait for Washington to organize every answer.

People who are hurting need more than sympathy. Supporting careful research gives their suffering the attention it deserves and offers a chance to move treatment beyond guesswork. Let that work begin now.

It’s six Eastern. It’s three o’clock Pacific. The President of Action, Coast to Coast and around the world, from the America Out Loud Talk Radio Studios. If you guys are serious about something you mean, it’s time for The Truth Be Told with Booker Scott.

Thousands of people still suffer today from vaccine injuries taken from the COVID vaccine. Before that, there were vaccine injuries of many types. What is the answer? How do we get help with this?

Because I’ve had many people on this program that have suffered from vaccine injuries. Her name is Dr. Irene Maverkakis. She’s a friend of mine, an associate, a colleague in Liberty, and we have her back on the program tonight. I’m Booker, and this is The Truth Be Told.

Irene, Dr. Irene Maverkakis, welcome back to the program. It’s great to have you. Hey, Booker. Well, thank you so much for having me on to discuss this important topic.

Yeah, it is important. And when the COVID vaccine came out and I think died suddenly, the whole died suddenly thing, I think it wasn’t real helpful because so many people thought that if you took the vaccine that you died. So many people thought if you took the vaccine then you got myocarditis. And that’s really just not even close to the truth.

But I think there are people that still believe that, and I think in some ways, people that claim to have a vaccine injury from COVID vaccine or any others. I believe that clouded the water for those people because you and I it’s your business, it’s what you do in the medical field. And I’ve had people on this program before that suffer from the COVID vaccine injury. We know that it’s real and it’s affecting people’s lives.

And I think all of that died suddenly stuff. I I think it hurt the people that are really hurt from vaccine injuries. And I’ve said this before when you’ve been on the program, you are someone that was vaxxing injured yourself many years ago. This was going back 13, 14 years ago.

Since that time, you have made it a part of your practice, and now you’re trying to get into it a little bit deeper to try to find some answers for these people that were injured during the COVID vaccine. Well, yeah, you make some good points. Yeah, I was vaccine injured in 2012 and was really sick for over eight years and found my way back to health from a combination of allopathic medicine and complementary and alternative medicine and some interesting nutritional changes. But I was a frequent flyer in the emergency room for a long time.

And inadvertently, through my practice as an interventional spine and musculoskeletal specialist, over the years, vaccine-injured patients will present as musculoskeletal or neurological pain, things like CIDP, which is chronic immune demyelinating polyneuropathy, it presents with pain and weakness in the legs, but often they get referred for a spine condition. And so over the years, I wound up figuring it out that some of these people are vaccine injuries. There’s a condition called adhesive capsulitis or frozen shoulder. But some of these people, the timeline is three weeks to three months after a vaccine, and it’s really shoulder injury related to vaccine administration or called server, and it’s a compensable vaccine injury on the traditional vaccine adverse event reporting system vaccine injury table, which of course we have this healthcare compensation fund to pay injuries because vaccine makers have product liability protection from a 1986 law.

So you make a lot of good points, to the extent by which if we focus too much on the people dying from them. But what I’ve been saying to people recently, and I think this is a good point, and you can tell me if you think it is or not. I will. If you all can accept people on daily medications that come into my office and they talk about, I think I’m having a side effect.

articles.title: Google’s AI glasses raise questions about enforcing biometric privacy protections
articles.content:
Google’s AI glasses raise questions about enforcing biometric privacy protections

Google is entering the AI glasses market with privacy protections designed to address controversies surrounding Meta’s smart eyewear. But its developer documentation leaves unanswered whether the operating system technically enforces its prohibition on facial recognition or relies on policing applications after they gain camera access. The question is whether the operating system enforces its prohibition on facial recognition or relies on policing applications after they gain access to the glasses’ cameras.

Google’s answer combines local facial redaction, restrictions on biometric identification, limits on AI training, and controls intended to prevent covert recording. Yet its Gemini assistant can visually analyze surroundings without illuminating an outward-facing recording indicator, a practice that has already attracted scrutiny of Meta’s glasses.

Google’s new intelligent eyewear, developed with Warby Parker, Gentle Monster, and Samsung, became available for preorder Thursday, with retail availability scheduled for December 10.

Privacy protections leave gaps

Google’s privacy measures include automatic redaction of bystanders’ faces before imagery reaches Gemini. Google says it does not save those visuals in Gemini History, use them for AI training, or use them for targeted advertising.

Google told 9to5Google that redaction occurs locally on the paired smartphone and that Gemini images are deleted immediately after processing. Whether unredacted frames persist temporarily in memory or diagnostic systems remains unverified.

The glasses require separate camera and microphone permissions, feature an outward-facing recording indicator with tamper detection, and limit conventional video recordings to 90 seconds. Google also plans to extend its Private AI Compute technology to the devices.

Its Android XR policies prohibit facial recognition, biometric identification, surveillance, real-time bystander identification, persistent eavesdropping, and voice identification.

The restrictions place Google’s platform in a different position from Meta, which has explored adding facial recognition to its smart glasses. Google is publicly prohibiting a capability its main competitor has explored, even as its developer documentation raises questions about how it technically enforces that prohibition.

Conventional photos and videos remain available without automatic anonymization, while Google’s published indicator requirements concern photos and videos saved to the gallery, rather than all camera-based Gemini interactions.

That mirrors the issue with Meta’s recording indicators.

Google’s approach reduces what Gemini can retain or infer about identifiable faces but does not necessarily notify someone whose image is being analyzed.

Camera access raises enforcement questions

Google’s Android XR hardware documentation explains how authorized third-party applications can access the glasses’ camera through a companion smartphone using standard Android CameraX interfaces, including ImageAnalysis.

The interfaces support computer vision and AI video processing. Applications must obtain separate permission to access the glasses’ camera, but permission controls and restrictions on subsequent biometric analysis are different mechanisms.

Google prohibits facial identification, yet its documentation does not identify a universal operating system control that automatically prevents an authorized application from analyzing camera imagery to identify someone. Nor does it establish that Gemini’s facial redaction applies to third-party applications.

Google requires apps to follow its intelligent eyewear safety rules, but its published documentation does not establish how those restrictions would be enforced against apps distributed outside Google Play.

The published camera interfaces concern Android companion devices; equivalent third-party access through an iPhone has not been established.

These unanswered questions do not demonstrate that unauthorized facial recognition can operate on the glasses. They mean Google’s documentation cannot independently establish the technical enforcement of its prohibition.

Meta’s controversies establish the stakes

Meta’s unreleased NameTag facial recognition system has drawn scrutiny, including a proposed class action alleging that Facebook and Instagram photographs were used to develop biometric identification capabilities without appropriate consent.

The allegations remain unproven. Meta acknowledged exploring facial recognition but said no feature had shipped to consumers and denied building a central facial recognition database.

The underlying concern is whether glasses that can identify strangers without their knowledge could turn ordinary encounters into opportunities for biometric surveillance. Google’s restrictions address that possibility directly, although the extent of their technical enforcement remains unclear.

The Texas attorney general also investigated Meta’s glasses over biometric privacy concerns. Google reached a $1.3 billion Texas settlement in 2025 over allegations involving location tracking, private browsing, and biometric information unrelated to its new eyewear.

Regulators question whether safeguards are sufficient

On October 29, Democratic Senators Edward Markey and Ron Wyden questioned Meta about sensitive imagery, AI training, recording indicator manipulation, and camera-based AI interactions without visible recording signals.

Meta has until November 25 to respond.

In May, ten Democratic senators led by Edward Markey and Jeff Merkley demanded that DHS abandon plans for biometric smart glasses that could enable immigration officers to identify people in real time without their knowledge or consent.

The proposed $7.5 million initiative, detailed in the Department of Homeland Security’s fiscal 2027 budget, underscores how wearable biometric identification is becoming both a government surveillance concern and a consumer privacy issue. Google’s restrictions directly address such uses, although their application to government or independently distributed software remains unverified.

The lawmakers’ concerns extend beyond consumer privacy to government surveillance, where Google’s restrictions on biometric identification could become particularly consequential.

Google’s safeguards address several of these concerns, but no established evidence shows they were developed in anticipation of oversight by the incoming Democratic Congress.

In an October 13 statement, the European Data Protection Board recommended obscuring bystanders’ identities, minimizing retention, and making AI-assisted camera processing noticeable to people nearby.

Its guidance recommends visual indicators that remain active long enough for bystanders to understand when imagery is captured for AI processing, not merely when conventional recordings are saved.

That creates a potential conflict with Google’s decision to leave its indicator inactive during Gemini visual inquiries, although the guidance does not establish that Google violates European data protection law.

Ireland’s parliamentary Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence went further in a November 10 report, recommending a prohibition on smart glasses capable of covert recording without consent.

The committee specifically cited concerns about Meta’s reported facial recognition plans while acknowledging the accessibility benefits of wearable visual assistance.

The Irish recommendation raises a more fundamental regulatory question than whether companies can improve privacy settings. It asks whether devices that can capture people without their awareness should be permitted in certain circumstances at all, regardless of the safeguards their manufacturers advertise.

The recommendation is not enacted law, and Google’s eyewear currently requires accounts from the U.S. or South Korea.

Google has shown that smart-glasses privacy safeguards can be built into hardware, operating system permissions, app policies, and AI processing.

What remains unresolved is how completely those controls prevent prohibited biometric identification after camera access is granted, and whether people standing in front of the glasses should have to rely on protections they cannot independently observe or control.

Article Topics

consumer electronics | data privacy | facial recognition | Google | smart glasses | wearables

articles.title: Lawmakers Race to Renew Warrantless Spying Before January
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

A group of US lawmakers is trying to convince Congress to use the lame-duck session to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA).

The idea is to add it to the must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) – and in this way bypass the incoming Congress, which is expected to be more privacy-friendly.

There is no time to waste: the House is scheduled to sit until December 17 and the Senate until December 18.

"My preference would be, let's just take the win that's on the table, get it done in the lame-duck," House Intelligence top Democrat Jim Himes is telling the press, while adding, "If that fails, we'll do something in the first quarter."

Senator Mike Rounds (R-SD) seems to be on the same page, noting that there is not enough time to deal with FISA separately, but it could be done if it is amended onto the NDAA.

"We don't have two weeks to work just on FISA," he said, and added, "If it's amended onto the NDAA then you can move forward and get it done in that time."

Himes and others want to rush the process in the hope of avoiding a new Congress that might try to add a warrant requirement to the new bill – and that, in their view, would be a step too far.

What 702 does is let US spy agencies collect communications of foreigners abroad without a warrant – and in the process, sweep up that of Americans as well. Those can then be searched by agents, again without a warrant, in what is known as backdoor search.

As Reclaim The Net reported in March, citing a ruling of the FISA Court, the FBI alone ran those searches more than 278,000 times in a single year.

"A supervisor's sign-off is not a warrant," we wrote at the time.

In the same ruling, the secret court said that the FBI had violated the US Constitution's Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches. The ruling was issued on March 17, and although the legal deadline to declassify it was September 13, it still remains secret.

Two senators, Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff, have said that the ruling covers how analysts can read Americans' messages without a warrant. The NSA, FBI, and CIA are all allowed to search the data collected under 702, and look for US persons' communications.

In a letter to the leaders of Congress, 27 civil society groups, led by Demand Progress, reminded lawmakers that 702 has been "abused to spy on protesters on the left and the right; 19,000 donors to a congressional campaign; members of Congress and their staff."

The letter, sent on November 12, asks that 702 is not attached to the NDAA or any other must-pass bill, and that the House and Senate have a proper debate on the matter.

Other lawmakers who want to see 702 reauthorized as soon as possible are Mark Warner (D-VA), vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and who believes that if that doesn't happen in the lame-duck session, "it becomes much more difficult in a new Congress."

Senator Mark Kelly (D-AZ) is also on board, saying, "We need to get it reauthorized... As soon as possible."

Senator James Lankford (R-OK) agrees, and believes the reauthorization should have happened "months ago."

Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) and former Biden administration official Adam Klein co-authored an op-ed published in the Wall Street Journal on November 12, titled, "A Vital National Security Tool Shouldn't Go Dark."

Himes is one of those who want to rush the process in the lame-duck session because, as he put it, "it's a political reality that the 702 that gets reauthorized with a Democratic House and Senate is going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the lame duck."

The "urgency" is not really there, since the statute lapsed at midnight on June 12, 2026, but the spying continues thanks to the FISA Court's annual certifications. At a July 15 Senate hearing, Sen. Mike Lee asked if the current authorization expires "until midnight on March 16 of 2027" - and the answer he received from Todd Blanche, then the attorney general nominee, was, "That is correct."

As Reclaim The Net reported in June, the "going dark" narrative is a myth - and that is because the FISA Court's authorization of 702 is good for a year, regardless of whether Congress acts or not.

Congress has used the NDAA to give 702 a short-term extension once before - in 2023.

The groups who signed the November 12 letter are not buying the argument that there is some urgency to pass the bill now, and that not doing it would leave the US in the dark.

The groups also point out that the claimed urgency presents "a false choice" and is "another scare tactic" - while in fact, "only 12 percent of Americans want FISA extended as-is."

Demand Progress executive director Hajar Hammado is unimpressed with Himes' efforts, saying, "Jim Himes has betrayed his own party and the American people."

Due Process Institute vice president Jason Pye said voters are "sick of backroom deals."

The Brennan Center for Justice at NYU School of Law's Hannah James is of the same opinion: "Slipping an extension into must-pass year-end legislation, instead of openly debating and voting on bipartisan reforms, would betray the democratic process and Americans' Fourth Amendment rights."

One of the groups who signed the letter, Color Of Change, was one of the main promoters of the 2020 "Stop Hate For Profit" Facebook ad boycott – which, as Reclaim The Net reported at the time, resulted in the tech giant bowing to the pressure and censoring more "hate speech."

It may seem strange that a group who pushed for more online censorship is now worried about the government's warrantless surveillance – but their stand on this issue is correct, and it doesn't erase their previous actions.

While Himes is wrong in saying that there is a win on the table in the lame-duck, he is right that the new Congress could add a warrant requirement - but that is the best argument for waiting, rather than rushing the process.

There is certainly no excuse to attach such a controversial provision to a defense bill – the question of whether the government should be able to read Americans' messages without a judge's approval has nothing to do with the NDAA, and everything to do with the Constitution.

articles.title: Biometric defenses put to the test with faster AI face-swap model
articles.content:
Biometric defenses put to the test with faster AI face-swap model

The best way to stop a face-swap attack may be to build a better one first. Sumsub and Constructor University‘s Bayes Group have announced ALADDIN, a generative AI model that produces realistic face swaps with 28 times fewer neural-network evaluations than a leading diffusion-based approach. They built it to attack biometric identity verification systems before criminals do. The model reaches top diffusion-level realism in a single step, and Sumsub says this cuts the time necessary for its red-team fraud simulations from days to hours.

A cheap, fast-growing threat

Face-swap attacks are cheap to make and hard to catch. According to Proof, a convincing live face swap takes about fifteen minutes to set up on a consumer laptop and costs roughly thirty cents a minute to run. In one case, an attack like this, combined with a stolen identity, passed DMV data and ID document checks and ended with the transfer of a property valued at $75,000 being completed. Unlike a prerecorded deepfake, a live swap turns its head, blinks and speaks on cue, and it is often fed in through a virtual camera, so it can get past the biometric presentation attack detection (PAD) checks built to stop it. Today’s tools also still struggle with head angles, eyewear, harsh lighting and age gaps between the ID photo and the live face.

Evidence of the growing threat is mounting. Sumsub found that sophisticated identity fraud grew 180 percent in a year. iProov reports that face-swap attacks rose 300 percent. Group-IB counted roughly 33 injection attack attempts a day against a single financial institution. ALADDIN is designed to help defenders get ahead of that curve.

Inside ALADDIN

ALADDIN stands for Adversarial LAtent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity SwappiNg. The team started with a high-capacity diffusion model, the class of model behind today’s most realistic image generators. These models build an image over many passes, which makes them slow and expensive to run at scale. The researchers used distillation to compress that multi-step process into a single operation. They kept the target subject’s pose, expression, lighting, background and anything partly covering the face, and transferred the source identity onto it.

Prof. Dr. Dmitry Vetrov, head of the Bayes Group, said the result surprised his team. They needed no complex distillation objective, he said: a strong diffusion model plus adversarial training on “that model’s own internal features” was enough to reach top quality “in a single network evaluation instead of 28.”

The research evaluates image-based face swapping rather than demonstrating an end-to-end live video injection attack against an identity verification system.

Rethinking face-swap benchmarks

The researchers also identified a bias in how face-swapping methods are evaluated. Until now, academic benchmarks tended to favor methods that were scored by the same models used to train them, which made the results look better than they were. The ALADDIN team re-evaluated existing methods with an independent scoring framework to set what they call a fair, objective standard. The researchers argue that their approach provides a fairer basis for comparing face-swap models, both in how quickly they generate realistic images and how accurately their quality is measured.

From days to hours

For Sumsub, the practical payoff is in red-teaming, where its engineers attack their own defenses before real fraudsters do. Vyacheslav Zholudev, Sumsub’s co-founder and CTO, said the team must “master the underlying technology down to its mathematical foundations.” He said that by generating swaps in a single step, ALADDIN lets Sumsub “simulate millions of complex edge cases” and harden its liveness defenses before new threats reach production.

Academia meets industry

ALADDIN is the first peer-reviewed result from Sumsub’s AI Academic Program, launched with Constructor University in September 2025. Vetrov said academia and industry need each other on deepfakes but usually work apart. Sumsub’s knowledge of how fraudsters actually use these models “rarely reaches a university lab,” he said.

The partnership is part of a wider trend. In October, Persona launched research grants of up to $100,000 each for university work on data privacy, fraud intelligence and accessible identity. These programs still face open questions about whether researchers can publish findings that are unfavorable to their sponsor, and how access to fraud data is governed.

Recognition and a staged release

The paper has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027. Because the tool could be misused, the release is staged. The research code is public on Hugging Face, alongside an open classifier built to detect ALADDIN-generated images. The model weights are available only through a gated application process for legitimate academic and defensive research.

The same efficiency that makes ALADDIN useful for defensive testing could also make sophisticated face swaps cheaper for attackers. That tension explains the restricted release of its model weights and reinforces the need for layered biometric and injection attack defenses.

Article Topics

AI fraud | biometric liveness detection | deepfakes | face biometrics | face swap | generative AI | Sumsub

articles.title: Podcast: EU and UK online safety laws keep coming. Are they making the internet safer?
articles.content:
Podcast: EU and UK online safety laws keep coming. Are they making the internet safer?

Online safety regulations are reshaping the internet as governments introduce new measures to reduce online harms. Two of the biggest targets are social media and adult content, with regulators slapping new requirements and guardrails on established platforms.

Both the EU and the UK are working on solutions in parallel. But as the sector matures, the specifics that differentiate the two streams – and the two regional approaches – are becoming more visible and entrenched in policy.

In the EU, the European Commission has called for a 12-month pause on draft national social media restrictions that overlap with its proposed EU Kids Act, seeking a harmonized approach across the bloc. But the European Digital Identity Wallet deadline is fast approaching, and the new world of wallets and digital credentials is set to shape the landscape in the near future.

Meanwhile, the UK continues to expand its online safety framework. New provisions of the Crime and Policing Act took effect on November 6, criminalizing possession and publication of certain pornographic material, with corresponding content moderation obligations for online platforms.

As all this legislation rolls out, the Biometric Update Podcast asks: is the internet getting safer? This episode features interviews with Irene Hernández, CEO of wallet-centric European age assurance provider Gataca; and Andy Lulham, COO of UK content moderation provider VerifyMy, weighing in on the issue from regional perspectives.

Will the EUDI Wallet come to dominate digital identity – and what about Google and Apple? Is AI a threat that will make illegal content easier to produce, or an essential tool for monitoring volumes of material beyond human capacity? Hernández and Lulham explore the questions.

Listen on: Spotify, Apple, YouTube, Podbean
