articles.title: Shufti patents split-inference age assurance with on-device biometrics
articles.content:
Shufti patents split-inference age assurance with on-device biometrics

Shufti has launched its on-device age verification tool. A release from the UK provider says the product combines on-device facial age estimation (FAE), encrypted age tokens and flexible verification methods, helping businesses confirm a user’s age eligibility without transmitting users’ facial images to a verification server.

Shufti has received U.S. Patent No. 12,749,342 B1 for its age verification technology covering an AI-based system that uses on-device facial analysis, split inference (SI), and encrypted One-Time Age Tokens (OTATs). Split-inference technology uses distributed neural computation to split AI processing between the user’s device and a secure verification server, optimizing efficiency and privacy.

Facial analysis begins on device

In split-inference models, edge devices process the initial layers before transmitting intermediate representations to a server. For age assurance, Shufti says, when a user begins an age check, its AI models analyze facial characteristics to estimate age and assess liveness locally, as a defense against spoofs and other presentation attacks.

The device then generates an encrypted One-Time Age Token containing intermediate AI outputs rather than the facial image. The server receives and validates the token, finishes AI processing, and determines whether the user meets the required age threshold.

Once the server completes verification, the business receives an age eligibility result without access to the user’s facial image or full identity details. The one-time token can be restricted to specific merchants and marked as used to prevent reuse.

The SI process makes it harder to reverse-engineer the age verification process or manipulate locally generated results.

Shahid Hanif, CEO of Shufti, says a business should not have to collect someone’s full identity to confirm whether they are old enough to access a service. “We developed this age verification solution to help businesses prevent underage access without requiring every legitimate user to provide higher assurance proof of age,” he says. “Our patented on-device AI age check approach keeps facial information on the user’s device while securely confirming age eligibility.”

Hanif says the patent marks “an important milestone in our efforts behind an approach that puts users’ data privacy at the centre of age verification.”

Shufti’s age assurance portfolio also includes risk-based schemes and products to address use cases across the risk and platform spectrum, offering facial age estimation, configurable age thresholds and confidence-based escalation, document verification for cases requiring additional proof, and biometric liveness detection certified to iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance.

articles.title: As automation scales, GLEIF positions vLEI as enabler of secure digital infrastructure
articles.content:
As automation scales, GLEIF positions vLEI as enabler of secure digital infrastructure

Developments in digital public infrastructure have primarily focused on identity for individuals, but as financial markets, cross-border commerce and digital services become increasingly automated, organizational identity is becoming an infrastructure issue. Businesses need a trusted way to establish their identity across borders and market infrastructures and prove who is authorized to act on their behalf.

The Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation, or GLEIF, believes globally verifiable organizational identity is the model that is needed to support finance and trade as AI agents move the economy toward automated transactions.

A legal entity identifier (LEI) is a unique 20-character alphanumeric code used to identify legal entities participating in financial transactions. Based on the ISO 17442 “Financial services — Legal entity identifier (LEI)” standard, it is intended to help identify legal entities on a globally accessible database, providing clear data about ownership. LEIs identify legal entities rather than individuals acting in a personal capacity. Thus, the public LEI data pool serves as a de facto global directory of non-individual participants in the financial market.

LEIs are issued by GLEIF-accredited organizations known as Local Operating Units (LOUs), which verify and maintain legal entity reference data.

Verifiable credential binds person to business

A digital extension of the LEI, the verifiable LEI or vLEI is the legal entity identifier in verifiable digital credential format. It uses cryptography to combine three identity sources: the entity’s identity as represented by its LEI, an individual’s personal identity, and the official organizational role they hold. This trinity of organization, person and role binds individuals to an organization and creates a cryptographically verifiable chain of credentials linked to an LEI record in the Global LEI Index.

The vLEI can be used in any kind of digital interaction, transaction or e-signature scenario – for instance, signing regulatory filings and reports, or authorizing business payments. As such, as wallet technology extends to encompass business wallet schemes such as the European Business Wallet (EBW), the vLEI could play a key role in anchoring the emergent digital public infrastructure in what GLEIF calls “the only open, standardized, and regulatory-endorsed legal entity identification system.”

The idea is to remove what GLEIF CEO Alexandre Kech describes in a recent article as a regulatory wall. “Currently, when a company in one country wants to pay, contract with, or onboard a company in another, it hits a wall of friction,” Kech writes. “Business registration data sits in national silos, in different languages and formats. No single, trustworthy way exists to confirm that a counterparty is real, legitimate, and genuinely represented by the people acting on its behalf.”

These regulatory barriers have consequences, says Kech, slowing trade, raising the cost of cross-border payments, creating openings for fraud and money laundering, and shutting out smaller organizations that can’t easily handle the administrative burden. “As more commerce moves online, the gap grows, and the need becomes more urgent: only verifiable organizations can participate fully in global markets.”

Project Aperta prototype with BIS demonstrates model in practice

As a proof of concept for interoperable business identity, GLEIF’s collaboration with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on Project Aperta illustrates how LEIs could reduce repeated identity checks and support cross-border financial services. Developed and run by BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre, it trialled an interoperability layer connecting existing open finance networks in the UK, United Arab Emirates, Brazil, Hong Kong and India.

This so-called ‘network of networks’ demonstrates how a combination of open finance data, payments frameworks, and the Global LEI System can simplify AML and KYC or KYB compliance, based on a common identity layer.

Agentic economy demands clear chain of trust

All of GLEIF’s arguments about the need to rethink organizational identity as shared infrastructure applied before AI agents took the stage; now, they have added urgency, as agentic AI’s infiltration of commerce makes the question of delegated authority central to functioning digital ecosystems. In any sustainable agentic economy, agentic actions must have accountability attached.

Says Kech in a GLEIF release, “any web of domestic networks that seeks to make legal entity data portable across borders needs a globally standardized system of verified organizational identity. The Global LEI System serves this purpose precisely: it helps infrastructure, businesses, and entities make verified business data as widely available as possible, globally.”

Speaking recently on the Biometric Update Podcast about digital finance for AI-driven economies and the role of the vLEI, Kech says that for agents, accountability, control and mandate must be clear – and defined against recognized standards. “The vLEI can bring that chain of trust between an entity, an individual who is accountable for an AI agent, an AI agent who is performing tasks within a specific mandate, all through chained credentials.”

Interoperability is the point

The meaning of infrastructure is changing, and its digitization, Kech argues, should not be taken as a natural evolution, but a concentrated and coordinated effort to improve how data, money and trade move across virtual and regulatory borders, anchored by a deep and established root of trust.

Digital public infrastructure, he writes, “is most powerful when its building blocks connect: a payment system is more valuable when it can identify who is being paid, and an identity scheme when it recognizes identities beyond its own borders.”

“Interoperability is not a feature added at the end; it is the whole point.”

articles.title: New York’s AI Rules: Confidential Reports, Daily Fines, and a Kill Switch Wish List
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

New York state is not wasting any time putting into practice the new rules that are to govern the development and deployment of AI there.

A portal, where the biggest AI companies must register, was opened on November 10 by the Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT).

DIGIT is a unit of the Department of Financial Services (DFS) that was given the task of overseeing the implementation of the RAISE Act, and this is the first step in putting that law into effect.

The RAISE Act was signed by Governor Kathy Hochul in December 2025, and amended in March 2026, to require that "large frontier developers" submit to the state a disclosure statement and pay a fee.

These companies must have had revenue of $500 million or more in the previous year, and the law gives them until January 1, 2027 to register. That is also the day the law takes effect.

The same day the portal was launched, Hochul also announced the opening of the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research (NYCAIRR), located at the State University of New York (SUNY) in Binghamton. The center is supposed to be independent, but it was launched by the governor and will work with the state to "inform policy decisions about AI safety and accountability."

No large frontier developer may "develop, deploy, or operate a frontier model, in whole or in part in New York state, without having a current disclosure statement filed with the office and paying the required share," the law says.

This means that the state is establishing a permanent reporting and control relationship with these companies, which will have to renew the disclosure statement every two years, and pay a pro-rata share of the costs of running the office.

The statement must contain the names of the company's offices in the state, three contacts, and owners of five percent or more of the company.

The companies must also publish a safety framework, and every three months send the office a confidential summary of risks arising from their internal use of their models. If the statement is missing or false, the office can fine them $1,000 a day.

The state is also requiring that all frontier developers - not only the large ones - report a "critical safety incident" within 72 hours.

The office can then pass these reports to "other governmental entities at their discretion" - and these reports are exempt from New York's public records law. The office is also empowered to adopt "additional reporting or publication requirements."

The Attorney General can seek civil penalties of $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for each subsequent one.

As for the NYCAIRR, the November 10 release announcing its launch said that "At the State's request, NYCAIRR will be able to provide expertise, assessments and evidence that can assist in informing state policy making and oversight of frontier AI Developers."

The center will also "coordinate with DIGIT to begin reviewing AI Developers' published safety frameworks and providing recommendations on ways to strengthen requirements."

The center has received $25 million in capital from the state and $30 million from donors, led by Tom Secunda, co-founder of Bloomberg LP, and who also chairs the board of the state's own AI network, Empire AI.

That project, which the center is part of, got $275 million in the 2024-25 state budget, and is described as "Governor Hochul's $500 million public-private initiative."

The RAISE Act specifically states that its provisions do not apply to "the Empire AI consortium or the institute." This means that the state's own AI project is exempt from the rules that the NYCAIRR will help shape.

In January, when the center was first announced, Hochul said it "will be an independent arm of research that gives New Yorkers transparency and confidence."

Its interim co-directors are Cornell Tech Dean Greg Morrisett and Columbia Executive Vice President for Research Jeannette Wing.

“One of the Center’s first objectives is a national recruiting effort for experts who focus on foundational limits and mathematical theory, formal methods and verification, agentic and complex systems, hardware security and privacy, interpretability and alignment, and scientific AI and biosecurity,” the release said.

DFS Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow said that her office looks forward to "working closely with the Center under Governor Hochul's leadership."

The November 10 release said that the governor would in the coming months "continue exploring ways to build on the RAISE Act as part of ongoing efforts to further strengthen New York's nation-leading AI safety laws and regulations."

At the same time, Hochul said that "Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable" - and added, "We're building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology."

In September, Hochul had a message for developers: "Bring it on. We will fight you in court, and we will hold you accountable," and mentioned that the state might "explore safeguards like AI kill switches if they're deemed feasible and in the best interest of our state."

At the time, the sponsor of the RAISE Act, Alex Bores, said that the office was empowered to "demand more data from AI companies, issue new rules, and recommend new legislation as the technology evolves."

As Reclaim The Net reported at the time, the law was all about creating "a permanent reporting and control relationship between the state and AI developers."

In October, Hochul signed a separate bill that will require age checks for chatbot users from January 1, 2027.

As the state is working to cement its position as a leader in regulating AI, the way it’s going about it is by keeping a file on every company that runs the systems millions of people use for writing, searching, and talking. The state will get reports from them that it can share with other governmental entities and keep secret, and it has the power to add to its demands by rule. And it has a center, funded by the state, that will help it come up with more rules, but is itself exempt from those rules. Registration is where control starts, not where it ends.

articles.title: The UK Considers Protecting Children From eBay by Checking Everyone’s Passport
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

UK’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has announced that the government is “looking seriously” at banning under 16s from using second-hand selling sites like Vinted and eBay – and the Sunday Times reports that Depop and Facebook Marketplace could also be added to the list.

“We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe,” Nandy said.

And what, pray, is the evidence for this? A three-year-old submission by The Children’s Society to a parliamentary inquiry into human trafficking, that mentions children being asked for “indecent photos in exchange for money” on Facebook Marketplace or Vinted.

No doubt this is a serious problem, but it’s hard to see how preventing 15-year-olds from selling their old jumpers on eBay would solve it.

The Sunday Times report says the government is worried about the messaging services on these platforms allowing “grooming” of children by strangers.

It’s not clear how the government plans to stop that, since the idea of the ban is to prevent under-16s from accessing these sites in the first place.

These are sites that already have their own rules in place – eBay says you must be 18 to use it, while Vinted requires users to be at least 18, and even asks for a document to prove it – a passport, driving license, student ID, public transport pass, or bank statement.

Depop allows 13-year-olds to sign up, and if they are under 18, they may be asked to provide “photographic ID and taxpayer information” in order to use PayPal and Depop Payments.

Facebook Marketplace says only adults can use it, and checks age with “a video selfie” or ID through Yoti.

eBay’s response to the latest news has been to say that “while the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more.”

The government’s proposal is not new – it was first announced in June as part of a broader push to keep under-16s off social media, and at that time, the list of “user-to-user platforms” that would be covered by the ban did not include “educational services, e-commerce platforms or music streaming.”

But now eBay is in the crosshairs, even though back in June, the government was assuring everyone that e-commerce sites were safe.

In September, Nandy promised “proper, comprehensive legislation” that would cover not just apps, but “the features that we believe are not safe”.

At the time, Nandy also said it was “uniquely wrong” that online spaces had been “policed and regulated only by the private sector” – and that seems to be the underlying message here: we don’t like the way you’re regulating, so we’ll take over.

The absurdity of the situation is not lost on observers, given that the rules that will apply to under-16s have not even been published yet – and the list of sites and services to be covered by the ban is already expanding.

While the government is not explaining its logic, it’s easy to follow – if the goal is to age-check everyone, then every site and service that allows messaging between users will have to be included.

To achieve this, every site will have to check the age of every user – which means that an adult selling a pram on eBay will have to have their age verified, just so that the site can be sure that no 15-year-old is selling their old bike.

There’s also “scope creep” – a term used by the Computer and Communications Industry Association’s Matthew Sinclair, who warned that the plan to restrict messaging between under-16s on social media “would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch.”

Ofcom has approved various methods that sites can use to check users’ ages, and these include photo ID matching, digital ID services, banking-based checks, and facial age estimation.

The regulator admits that 16- and 17-year-olds without photo ID “would likely need to take steps to obtain one.”

What about adults? They will be subjected to an even wider variety of checks, such as credit card, mobile network, and email-based checks.

The government’s plan is to introduce the new rules in March 2027.

In September, we reported that Nandy said companies could be removed from the list of those subject to the rules if they “change” – but at this point, it’s unclear what kind of “change” would satisfy the government, or how a site or service would “prove” it had changed.

At the same time, the minister revealed that the rules would start applying in March 2027, while in October, a government “fact sheet” said that proving you are over 18 could be “as simple as a facial recognition check.”

When the UK finally introduced age checks for adult sites in July 2025, some VPN providers reported an 1,800% increase in signups.

The idea that a ban that has not yet been written, or explained, is already growing in scope – from social media to second-hand clothes and beyond – is a chilling thought.

It means that every expansion will require even more passports, face scans, and ID checks of adults – who just want to sell a coat. The children were never the ones being checked.

articles.title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
articles.content:
AI abuse by cybercriminals may be ramping up the volume and velocity of attacks, but the attack chain has yet to be radically transformed from conventional methods.

AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

Even in the most high-profile example of an AI powered attack to date, in which Claude Code was abused by Chinese state-sponsored actors to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025, conventional attack techniques and procedures laid the foundation, with AI abused as an enabler to support reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data analysis, and exfiltration during the GTG-1002 campaign.

JadePuffer, a ransomware campaign disclosed in July 2026, witnessed an LLM-driven agent automating most of the intrusion chain. Initial exploitation was through CVE-2025-3248, a year-old missing-authentication flaw in Langflow, a popular open-source framework for building LLM applications and agent workflows.

Vulnerable internet-facing Langflow instances were looted for cloud credentials, API keys, and other secrets before lateral movement, privilege escalation, and ultimately destructive database encryption.

JadePuffer shows AI’s potential for automating conventional attack methods, but it also underscores how vulnerable software is where AI has been giving attackers the biggest edge to date. AI tools can readily find exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders can patch them, a huge problem for the many enterprises carrying years of technical debt. And security experts see software flaws rising as a root cause of breaches as a result.

What AI enables

In addition to enhancing attackers’ flaw discovery prowess, AI is also enabling attackers to fail or succeed faster. Defenders are witnessing improvements in speed, scale, and operational ability from attackers that correlates strongly with increasing capabilities of AI tools.

“Adversaries are realizing the same gains in development velocity and operations that everyone else is getting from implementing AI,” says Darren Meyer, security research advocate at application security tools vendor Checkmarx.

Black Duck’s Lewis sees this expanding attackers’ reach and empowering more attack experimentation.

“An attacker can potentially investigate more opportunities, try more approaches, and move to the next target at a pace that would be difficult for a human team to match,” he says.

That in turn will increasingly alter a pivotal phase of conventional attack patterns that traditional favors defenders, notes Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at cloud security firm Sysdig.“That dwell time, which was often weeks or months, was where detection happened,” she says.

Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait.

‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization

By leveraging agentic AI in their operations, hackers can also draw on a deeper pool of domain expertise — database administration, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — compared to human attack teams where different people tend to specialize in different things such as web app security or malware development.

“Think of it as a database admin, a developer, an IT engineer, a DevOps specialist, a cloud architect, and a hacker combined into a single role,” says Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO and founder of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense. “We call it agentic APT, and the critical shift is that it is no longer exclusive to nation-state actors.”

Tymoshyk adds: “A threat that previously required a coordinated team of specialists can be deployed by a single person with the right prompt and the right model.”

Security researchers, including UnderDefense, report that attackers favor Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, which have significantly fewer content restrictions, rather than their more restricted Western alternatives as a platform to mount attacks.

“Attackers switch between models depending on what the task requires: one for reconnaissance, one for code generation, one for crafting social engineering content,” Tymoshyk says. “The modularity is part of the attack design.”

Attackers often prefer to use local models both because of operational security advantages and because some models may have weaker safeguards against malicious use.

Other experts cautioned that the abuse of particular models is difficult to determine and, in any case, a side issue to the main problem of defending against attacks.

“Attribution of particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation from very thin evidence on the ground,” says Checkmarx’s Meyer. “True attribution can only come from infiltration of threat groups or compromise of threat group infrastructure, both of which are rarely available to public researchers.”

The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining.

AI attack economics

The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI.

“A human attacker builds a playbook per campaign and reuses it, so every new target costs engineering time to make adjustments,” says Sysdig’s Morin. “An agentic threat actor carries context about a whole class of applications and composes its plan live against whatever it finds. There, the only cost is inference budget. And as running a complex attack gets cheaper, the number of attempts will go up.”

Agentic attacks are still flawed, and breadth of expertise is a poor substitute for depth of knowledge.

“Agents hallucinate and are noisy, which is often why they’re catchable,” notes Sysdig’s Morin. “Jadepuffer had flaws in its ransom note, encryption, wallet, and data exfiltration. There are still many areas in which human analysis and skill still outperform agent memory.”

Countermeasures

“The core objectives of the threat actor haven’t really changed, but the timeframe for a successful attack has been compressed dramatically,” says Nathan Smolenski, CISO at vulnerability management and compliance firm Qualys. “Frontier AI tools accelerate vulnerability discovery and weaponization, shrinking the window between disclosure and exploitation to near zero.”

Smolenski adds: “Defenders can no longer rely on traditional, human-speed 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets.”

AI significantly changes the entry dynamic by expanding the attack surface — particularly through end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents.

In response, defending organizations must shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defences while still keeping on top of foundational security defenses such as patching and authentication controls.

“Implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails enables security teams to automate lower-level triage efforts and focus human expertise on governing agents, validating outputs, and making more critical risk decisions,” Smolenski concludes.

articles.title: Nine healthcare lies and the rights you’ve surrendered
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Americans have been told their medical information is protected, their health insurance guarantees access to care, and their doctors are making decisions based on what is best for them. Twila Brase has spent decades examining the laws and policies behind those assurances. What she has uncovered raises serious concerns about who controls American healthcare and how much authority patients have already surrendered.

Following the recent U.S. election, the growing sense of political defeat is becoming difficult to ignore. Dr. Sherri Tenpenny and Twila Brase examine the discouragement spreading among voters who have lost confidence in their ability to influence government decisions. Younger Americans are facing an increasingly uncertain future, burdened by financial pressures and a political establishment that appears disconnected from their circumstances. Brase describes conversations with young voters who question whether participating in elections can accomplish anything. That resignation carries consequences for a country whose citizens are becoming increasingly convinced that the institutions governing their lives are beyond their control.

At a recent Freedom Summit in Minnesota, Brase delivered a presentation identifying nine claims about American healthcare that she considers fundamentally misleading. Her examination begins with the distinction between health insurance and managed health plans, exposing the authority insurers retain to determine which treatments patients can receive. She challenges the stated affordability objectives of Obamacare and examines the extensive sharing of personal medical information permitted under HIPAA. Patients routinely sign privacy acknowledgments with little understanding of the permissions already granted to the institutions holding their records. The legal framework governing those records extends far beyond the examination room.

Electronic health records introduce another level of institutional control. Brase describes government certification requirements that helped reshape medical recordkeeping and created systems capable of exchanging patient information across healthcare networks. She then examines ambient listening technology, which can capture conversations during medical appointments and generate clinical documentation through automated interpretation. Her examples include medical histories assigned to the wrong patients and serious medical events appearing in records where they never occurred. Physicians can face considerable difficulty correcting these errors, leaving patients exposed to the consequences of information they never provided.

The financial structure surrounding medical care creates additional pressure. Brase describes how employer-sponsored health plans consume substantial compensation while patients remain subject to coverage restrictions. She recounts a patient quoted $40,000 for surgery at one hospital who subsequently obtained a $3,600 price from another facility. The original hospital then offered to match that price. Her proposed alternative would return purchasing authority to patients through direct payment and catastrophic insurance coverage, challenging the financial relationships that currently determine access to treatment.

The conversation reaches an especially disturbing issue involving children receiving vaccinations while under general anesthesia. Dr. Tenpenny references reports dating to 2010, while Brase raises concerns about informed parental consent and the difficulty of distinguishing a possible vaccine reaction from complications associated with anesthesia or surgery. The discussion exposes another area where medical decisions may be influenced by institutional incentives, leaving parents dependent on the completeness of information provided before their children enter the operating room.

The nine claims Brase challenges expose unresolved questions about the authority institutions exercise over medical decisions Americans believe remain their own.

Meet the Guest

Twila Brase is the president and co-founder of Citizens’ Council for Health Freedom, a Minnesota-based organization that has challenged government interference in medical decisions since 1998. She is the author of Big Brother in the Exam Room: The Dangerous Truth About Electronic Health Records, an examination of medical data collection and the systems influencing physician independence. Brase works to protect the confidential patient-doctor relationship and restore individual control over healthcare decisions. Her organization is currently advancing its 3C Center for Health Freedom initiative, focused on cash payments, catastrophic coverage, and charity.

Learn more at CCHFreedom.org.

Tenpenny Prime Membership

It’s a place where we can examine complicated health issues, explore research, and continue asking questions through educational presentations and live discussions with experts. Explore Tenpenny Prime or become a member at primemembership.drtenpenny.com

The Tenpenny Files airs on weekdays at 3 pm ET on America Out Loud Talk Radio. Listen on iHeart Radio, our world-class media player, or our free apps on Apple, Android, or Alexa. All episodes of The Tenpenny Files can be found on podcast networks worldwide, the day after airing on talk radio.

Transcript Summary of this podcast episode ⤵

The most important relationship in medicine is being crowded out. Between the patient and the doctor stand insurers, government rules, corporate employers, and computer systems. Patients pay more while surrendering control over decisions that belong to them.

That is the central failure our healthcare debate keeps overlooking. Changing who pays the bill will not restore freedom if someone else still controls the care.

Consider what happens when patients can shop. Health freedom advocate Twila Brase recounts an uninsured Georgia man quoted $40,000 for prostate surgery. After finding a $3,600 price at the Surgery Center of Oklahoma, he told the Georgia hospital he would travel. The hospital offered to match that price.

One account cannot describe every medical situation. It does expose the power of a patient who knows the price and can take his business elsewhere.

Control also means knowing what happens to our most personal information. HIPAA permits many disclosures without individual authorization. A privacy notice should never be mistaken for a promise that information stays between patient and physician.

Electronic records and ambient listening tools raise questions. Who receives the information? Who checks computer-generated notes for errors? Can patients decline recording? A confidential appointment should not quietly become a data collection exercise.

Brase’s proposed way back rests on three principles: cash, catastrophic coverage, and charity. Routine care would be purchased directly. Insurance would protect against major expenses. Charity would help people unable to pay.

The goal is to put purchasing power in patients’ hands and make doctors answer to the people seeking their help.

That vision deserves attention from families exhausted by premiums, deductibles, and permission slips. Healthcare should be an affordable, confidential relationship between a patient and a trusted physician. Restoring that relationship is the work ahead. Freedom in medicine begins when patients regain control of their care.

And for example, I heard one story about the doctor happened to mention his own problem with his own back, right? And it got listed as though the patient had said that they were having back pain. And so this thing can happen because this is just a computerized system that’s picking this all up and figuring out how it should go together.

And so a lot of people don’t understand ambient listening and they think it’s just a recorder, but it’s it is a third person in the room in a confidential conversation, listening to every word. And then there’s also a company behind that. So you have to think very carefully what you want to do. And so this is just something that was on the line on on a website talking about how it organizes, summarizes, and creates paragraphs and headers in the electronic health record in the EHR note structure.

And it can decide that something you said is not appropriate to talk about. So you came in to talk about your toe, and and you just happen to start talking about your headache. Well, it it decides, the computer decides that no, that’s not that’s not necessary to be added to the electronic health record. So the doctor has to try and remember that you said something about a headache and put it in later.

And so here’s just a few stories. I’ll I’ll say so this this one woman came in to review her lab work from a time where it was being recorded through ambient listening. And she came in, the doctor started to go over her last visit, which was recorded. And the patient said, No, that’s that’s not me.

The doctor said, Oh, yeah, that’s you. Let me just say a few more things here. And the patient said, No, that’s not me at all. And so what was discovered is that the computer system had plopped this woman’s history of her last visit into somebody else’s record and had put somebody else’s record into her record.

And so this is what the computer can do. Another story is a doctor told the story about his patient who came into the emergency room and it’s recorded that his patient was in full respiratory arrest. CPR was being given, but the fact of the matter is his patient came in for high blood pressure, never was under a respiratory arrest, and he’s as a doctor is having a hard time changing the record, making the record accurate. And then another time a woman told me about her friend who was in, and the whole thing was, and they both knew the doctor and the patient knew that the ambient listening was at work, the recording was happening.

And when the doctor said, Okay, you’ve got this condition, and so you, let me offer you this service or this, treatment. But be would you like this treatment? But before she could say anything, he he started shaking his head silently, shaking his head and going like this, to basically tell her to say no. Clearly, he did not feel comfortable telling her to say no, and he had to offer this treatment, but he didn’t think it was a very good idea for her.

So this is it might, what we say is know what what’s going on, ask every time about whether or not you’re being recorded, make a decision, like say, no, I don’t want to be recorded, please shut that off. And understand that it might be also for the doctor’s benefit, but also for yours. Well, what will the doctor tell you, or would the doctor tell you if the doctor wasn’t being recorded? And then I told you about all the different places, places it could be, and you might be notified about it, you might not be notified about it, you might be notified about it just as the doctor leaves the room.

Oh, I forgot to tell you that you were being recorded. Or it could be a sign up on the on the wall, but you’re so busy being in pain or dealing with your children, you don’t even notice it. But those signs say if you stay in this room, you have agreed to be recorded. All right, line number six, the provider is a provider, is a provider.

That’s not true, but the entire corporate healthcare system is trying to move from a medical model to a nursing model, replacing physicians with nurse practitioners or with physician assistants. And all these practitioners are have their own purpose and their own place. But the fact of the matter is the corporations are seeing that they can pay these non-physicians less, have the non-physician follow the electronic health record for what should be done. And and then they’ll just be, they won’t have to pay a physician, but you also won’t get the expertise of a physician.

But that’s again moving from a medical model to a nursing model. And you should actually want to have the access to a physician who has had so many more years and so many thousands of hours more of experience and expertise and training. All right, line number seven: employer-sponsored coverage is a benefit that is not true. It’s actually a theft.

People don’t think of it this way, but they should think of it this way. So $28,000 is the latest number for a family of four that you’ll have to spend every year. The employer spends about $17, $18, or even $20,000 of that, and the employee will tack on another six or seven, and then in addition to that, there’ll be the deductible, right? But imagine what you could do if you had the full amount that your employer gets sends to that health plan, which again is not insurance, right?

It can deny you access to care. Imagine if you had that full amount, $15,000, $20,000, whatever it is, and then tack on your amount, and you’ve got, $28,000 that you could decide what to do with. Because at the end of the year, $28,000 goes away, even if you never use one dime of healthcare. You should really get your full compensation.

That’s something our organization is going to drive toward in our policy work. Here is it in a diagram, and this is from 2023. But as I said, the number that’s out now is 2020, 2000, sorry, $28,000, not $24,000. And here, when you think about how you could use that money and still be covered, you could consider healthcare sharing, which the this is the price that you could pay for healthcare sharing per month for you as an individual or for your entire family, if that works for you.

There, and then of course, we want the entire country to go back to catastrophic coverage, where in 2007, the the guy who owns Sano surgery on in a text, he said, back then I had real catastrophic health insurance, and we were paying $149 a month for a $10,000 deductible and $3.8 million in coverage. That’s where we need to go back to. All right, line number eight: Medicare for All is the solution for healthcare. It is totally not the solution for healthcare.

Medicare itself is in trouble. 10,000 baby boomers enter every day. Asset depletion is expected in 2033. Six years from now, only 89% of the bills would be paid.

If that were the case in 2022, 99.5 billion dollars would not have been paid. And thus the ration of care, which is already taking place, will take place in a far greater amount to seniors who will not be able to do anything to stop the rathing that’s coming. And lie number nine, the last fly. Sherry said there’s a surprise.

Well, yes, because I just had to throw this one in. When the Freedom Summit asked for this, I thought I’ve just got to say this lie because this is such a big lie. Ivermectin is dangerous, it’s totally not dangerous. And as a matter of fact, here’s just a case study everybody should keep in their back pocket to report whenever anybody says ivermectin is dangerous.

And this came from a case study out of Cameroon. A 19-year-old woman in Cameroon decided to use ivermectin to commit suicide. She had taken 400 pills by the time that she was found. She was hospitalized five days with an IV just to maintain her until all of that medication left her system and all of the symptoms subsided.

There was no major organ damage, and she recovered and she’s studying at the university. So 400 pills, the three milligram version. Ivermectin is not dangerous. So those are the nine lives versus the nine truths.

And and I just like to say this is a battle we cannot afford to lose over the practice of medicine in America because it will determine your life, it will determine your liberty. And so, as we were talking about before, and I’ll just breeze through this the way back to health freedom is cash catastrophic coverage and charity, our 3C solution. And just so you understand, today the payers on the top, the patient and the doctor are on the bottom. Everybody waits for the payer to decide what the government, the employer, the health plan is going to do.

But in the future, in our 3C solution, the insurer will pay you, the patient, and you’ll take all the money from the insurer, from your bank account, from your pocket, wherever it has to come from, to pay the doctor in the hospital yourself. And every price will come down to the cash-based level where they still profit. That story about the $40,000 versus the $3,600. Dr. Key Smith at the surgery center was not going in debt for that payment.

He was still making a profit, which shows you what can happen if you’re in a cash-based and all the three, all the third parties get out of the way and stop grabbing all of the money. So that’s the solution to make healthcare affordable, bring freedom back, and fix healthcare. And then here’s just some of our helpful handouts. And I told you where to go.

You can use the QR code if you’d like to donate for our $50,000 match. We would love your help. We need your help to get all those $50,000. And and you can also go to our Substack, the Health Freedom Dispatch.

We have a brand new Substack out. And for the life of me, I forget now what the what it’s about, but it’s there. And oh, it’s about the election. That’s what it is.

And here’s my book, and here’s the privacy, please. No ambient listing. You can get this at the helpful handouts. Take this with you to the doctor’s office.

Either hang in on the door and just show it to the doctor, ask the questions about ambient listening while you decide whether you want to be recorded or not. Whoop. And then here we are. Here’s me.

That’s it. And I will stop sharing. Well, Twila, like always, everything that you have to present is just so important and so valuable. And I hope that people who’ve listened to this will take the time to re-listen to it and maybe even take notes because there’s it’s really important to know what those nine lies are and what to do about them and what they really mean.

I think the thing about HIPAA when I first met you many, many years ago, was one of the most shocking things that I found out about what did you say, 22 million people? 2.2 million. And one 1.5 million of those are business associates. Business, nothing to do with your healthcare at all.

Wow. Well, I think that so when they make such a big deal of you signing that little piece of paper when you go into the doctor’s office, and and it’s and you think that that’s to protect you, and it’s really not. And so this information is really, really valuable. Well, we’ve got a few minutes left now before the end of our of our time together here this month.

There was a there’s a big thing that came out about the vaccinating kids under anesthesia, and it’s certainly a health freedom issue that I’m sure that your organization has talked about. And I’ve I’ve been in the process of putting together, I’ve I’ve just got so many writing projects I need to get to. I want to write an article about this because did that the first reported case of vaccinating kids under anesthesia was in 2010? And this has been going on for quite some time, 25 years.

And I guess that now that they’ve gone through the billing records and they see how much money the hospitals are actually making from doing this, I think that people don’t realize that this has been a long-standing problem. And I think it’s even more of a problem since COVID. What have you guys been talking about about this issue? So, my question back in 2010 is did they ask the parents and and say, for I think that’s just the first thing.

Do you want us to give your child a vaccine while your child is under anesthesia? So, first of all, there just should be consent, but second of all, there should be informed consent. When this all just broke in the news, not all that long ago, it was interesting to see the comments of anesthesiologists who are concerned. Of course, there’s the anesthesiologists who say, well, this is just a great thing.

We get more children vaccinated, right? But there’s the anesthesiologists who say, Well, if there’s something happening to that child under anesthesia, are we going to recognize if it’s from the reaction to the vaccination or is it from the reaction to what’s happening in the surgery and the anesthesia itself? And that’s one where I think, if you think of a vaccine as just negligible, like, it’s as harmless as taking a sip of water, okay, but it’s not. It’s not.

And, to mix these kinds of things in a time when the child can’t even respond, and now you’re all trying to figure out what the physiological signs are, whether they’re about the surgery or the vaccine, it just doesn’t seem wise to me. And clearly to these anesthesiologists, it didn’t. But they are saying that they’re asking the parents, but are they fully informing the parents about this a problem? Yeah, it’s one thing to give informed consent about the vaccine under normal circumstances, but what about the vaccine with all of those ingredients, depending on which vaccine they’re talking about?

All those ingredients that are given when the person get under general anesthesia is getting all kinds of other drugs with it to keep them, anesthetized and keep them in a semi-comatose position for the surgery. We don’t I don’t even know that we have any data on that. Like looking at mice that are under general anesthesia and we give them a vaccine. I mean, what happens?

I don’t even know that that even those levels of experiments have been done with this. I think it’s just criminal. It’s just one more way that physicians in this country are just needle wielding, like like I always think of them when you think about Einstein’s picture with his gray hair all up around, he looks crazy. I think physicians are like that.

Needle, wheel, needle wielding, just inject, inject, inject, inject, vaccinate, vaccinate, vaccinate. Well, two things about that is right, we have discovered how little research there is even on mice for these for these vaccines. So, really, how informed of a consent is that to the parents?

But also, your listeners may or may not realize that now it’s about 80% of the doctors who are employees, employees. And so if the vaccines are bringing in so much money to the corporations that employ these these doctors, and if a lot of these doctors are still facing these huge loans from medical school, right? articles.title: After a Stroke: 4 Common Challenges and How Rehabilitation Can Help
articles.content:
One afternoon, a 65-year-old retired civil servant did not wake up from his nap. When his wife checked on him, she found that he had lost control of his bladder and bowels. He was rushed to the hospital and diagnosed with an ischemic stroke.

After a month in the hospital, he could walk with a quad cane and was discharged.

However, the previously sociable man developed aphasia (a language disorder), which significantly affected his ability to communicate. His speech became slurred, and he could no longer understand what others were saying or read written text. As a result, he had to stop volunteering.

After about four months of speech and language rehabilitation, he could finally hold simple conversations and spend time with friends.

Chun-Ping Wang, director of Runsheng Rehabilitation Clinic in Taiwan, shared the case with The Epoch Times.

The first three to six months after an ischemic stroke are a critical window for rehabilitation, Wang said. During this period, the brain exhibits increased neuroplasticity, allowing neural pathways to reorganize more efficiently and supporting a more favorable recovery process.

The effects of an ischemic stroke vary depending on the region of the brain affected, so rehabilitation must be tailored to each person.

4 Common Challenges After an Ischemic Stroke

Four of the most common aftereffects of an ischemic stroke and their corresponding rehabilitation strategies are:

1. Limb Weakness and Unsteady Walking

Dr. Pin-Yuan Chen, a professor and attending neurosurgeon at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taiwan, told The Epoch Times that hemiplegia (paralysis on one side of the body) and movement impairment are among the most common complications of ischemic stroke.

When the areas of the brain responsible for movement are damaged, patients may experience weakness in the arm and leg on one side, muscle stiffness, and poor coordination. In the early stage of the stroke, some may be almost completely paralyzed.

Task-oriented training is commonly used to improve balance, postural control, walking speed, and endurance, Wang said.

Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation is a rehabilitation technique that uses movements such as squatting, reaching, and controlled breathing to help patients relearn how to control their limbs.

When combined with electrical stimulation, it can further promote muscle contraction and increase range of motion. It helps patients perform larger movements, thereby building confidence in rehabilitation.

2. Speech and Language Difficulties

When an ischemic stroke affects the brain’s language network, communication between the brain and the muscles involved in speech may be disrupted, potentially leading to aphasia, Chen said.

Melodic intonation therapy can be used to address language difficulties.

The therapy uses melody and rhythm to retrain speech and helps patients practice breath control, articulation, and speech rhythm, gradually improving their ability to communicate.

On “Health 1+1” on NTD, a sister outlet of The Epoch Times, Kuo-Pin Wu, director of XinYiTang Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Clinic in Taiwan and a contributor to The Epoch Times, described a 48-year-old patient who had severely slurred speech after a stroke. The patient was deeply discouraged by his symptoms.

Wu instructed him to sing at least five songs every day, joking, “If you don’t sing five songs, don’t come back to see me.”

The patient began singing with his wife every day at home. Over time, he found that singing not only helped him relax but also gradually improved his speech and language abilities.

3. Choking and Swallowing Difficulties

If the nerves that control swallowing are damaged, patients may cough or choke while eating and drinking, increasing the risk of aspiration pneumonia (lung infection when food or liquid enters the lungs), Chen said. This issue should not be overlooked and requires prompt attention.

These patients may benefit from resistance exercises for the swallowing muscles, Wang said. By strengthening the tongue, jaw, and throat, these exercises may help improve swallowing function.

4. Depression and Cognitive Decline

Emotional changes are among the most easily overlooked complications of stroke, Chen said. These changes are not solely a psychological response to the loss of physical function. Damage to neural circuits in the brain can also impair emotional regulation.

Some patients may also experience memory loss, difficulty concentrating, and declines in judgment and executive function. In severe cases, these can progress to vascular dementia, a decline in thinking and memory caused by reduced blood flow to the brain.

The key factors influencing rehabilitation outcomes include starting rehabilitation during the critical recovery window, engaging in goal-directed and repetitive training, and the patient’s willingness to actively participate, Wang said.

Support and encouragement from family members can play an important role in helping patients stay motivated and adhere to their rehabilitation over the long term. After leaving the hospital, continuing regular rehabilitation, getting enough sleep, maintaining proper nutrition, and adjusting the rehabilitation plan as needed can all help support ongoing recovery.

TCM as a Complement to Stroke Rehabilitation

In addition to the rehabilitation methods described above, TCM may be used as an adjunctive therapy following an ischemic stroke.

Chou Tsung-han, chief physician of Ming Tang Clinics in Taiwan, told The Epoch Times that, from a TCM perspective, stroke is not viewed solely as a sudden event but as the result of long-term imbalances in the body.

TCM treatment is individualized and focuses on restoring balance in organ function and rebuilding physical strength, helping patients sustain the energy required for rehabilitation and everyday activities.

Acupuncture is often used in TCM to support blood flow to the brain, thereby aiding muscle responsiveness and neurological recovery.

Commonly used acupoints include:

Hundred Meetings (Bai Hui, GV20)

The Hundred Meetings acupoint is located on the midline at the top of the head, in a slight depression approximately at the level of the tips of the ears.

Four Mind Alertness (Si Shen Cong, EX-HN1)

Four Mind Alertness consists of four points located approximately one thumb-width in front of, behind, and on either side of the Hundred Meetings acupoint.

Dietary Therapy for Stroke Recovery

Gastrodia rhizome is commonly used in TCM to address transient cerebral ischemia (mini stroke) and support stroke prevention, Chou said.

Chou recommends the following dish as part of a daily diet during stroke recovery:

Chicken Soup With Gastrodia and King Oyster Mushrooms

This medicinal soup may be suitable during recovery after an ischemic stroke and as part of a regular diet to help support brain health.

Servings:6

Soak Time:2 hours

Prep and Cook Time:1 1/2 hours

Total Time:3 1/2 hours

Ingredients

  • 10 grams gastrodia rhizome

  • 50 grams dried black fungus

  • 500 grams king oyster mushrooms

  • 1 stewing hen

  • 4 quarts water

  • 8 grams salt

  • Ginger slices, scallion sections, and ground pepper, to taste

Instructions

  • Soak the gastrodia rhizome in water for 30 minutes. Soak the dried black fungus for two hours until rehydrated. Slice the king oyster mushrooms. Clean the stewing hen and cut it into pieces.

  • Pour the water into a pot and add the black fungus, king oyster mushrooms, chicken, ginger slices, and scallion sections.

  • Bring to a boil over high heat and continue to boil for five minutes.

  • Reduce the heat to low, add the gastrodia rhizome, and simmer for one hour.

  • Season with salt and pepper before serving.

Note:Because gastrodia rhizome is a medicinal herb, pregnant women and people taking medications should consult a physician before taking it regularly.

Some herbs mentioned in this article may be unfamiliar, but they are generally available in health food stores and Asian grocery stores. It is important to note that treatment methods may vary depending on the person. Please consult with a healthcare professional for a specific treatment plan.

articles.title: New York City votes to ban surveillance pricing
articles.content:
Two people shopping for the same product shouldn’t have to wonder whether one is paying more because a company knows more about them.

That’s the concern behind a bill passed by the New York City Council on November 12. The legislation targets surveillance pricing, defined as using personal data and algorithms to offer different people different prices for the same goods or services.

Introduction 891-A would prohibit these practices in transactions with consumers in New York City. It would also restrict collecting, selling, or sharing personal data to facilitate surveillance pricing. The bill is at the mayor’s desk and would take effect one year after becoming law.

For consumers, the issue goes beyond an unexpectedly expensive shopping cart. It’s about companies turning information about your life and online behavior into a tool for deciding what to charge you.

Learn more about surveillance pricing in this episode of our podcast Lock & Code:

Large-scale data collection also creates risks beyond pricing, including sensitive inferences about people and unauthorized disclosure of their information.

What exactly is surveillance pricing?

Surveillance pricing uses information about you, or a profile a company has built about you, to help determine the price you see for a specific product or service.

That information can include your location, browsing history, shopping habits, and demographic characteristics. In initial findings published in January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said pricing tools could draw on surprisingly detailed behavior, including mouse movements and the products people leave unpurchased in their online shopping carts.

This is not some conspiracy theory. There is evidence that the tools and data pipelines exist. The FTC’s findings drew on documents from pricing and technology intermediaries. Staff reported that the intermediaries examined worked with at least 250 clients across sectors including groceries and apparel. The published examples were hypothetical to protect confidential business information.

Surveillance pricing should not be confused with dynamic pricing. Dynamic pricing can respond to changing market conditions, such as demand or availability. Surveillance pricing uses personal information to differentiate between customers. While the two can overlap, they aren’t interchangeable.

A personalized price isn’t automatically a higher price. Some shoppers might receive discounts. The concern is that an opaque pricing system gives sellers detailed insight into customers while those customers are unable to see how they’re being assessed.

Another form of unequal pricing that the bill allows is qualifying loyalty and other discounts. The bill preserves genuine discounts, including qualifying loyalty and rewards programs and discounts for clearly defined groups such as veterans, seniors, and teachers. But those exceptions come with conditions.

Surveillance pricing doesn’t necessarily charge wealthy shoppers more and give everyone else a break. Pricing tools can estimate what you’re willing to pay, which may have little to do with what you can comfortably afford. Perceived price sensitivity is a deciding factor, so a wealthy bargain hunter could receive a discount, while someone with less money but an urgent need or few alternatives could be judged willing to pay more.

For consumers, the underlying question about surveillance pricing is straightforward: How much does the price reflect what’s being sold, and how much does it reflect what a company thinks it can get out of you?

New York City’s bill aims to limit how companies use your personal information to make that calculation.

Your name, address, and phone number may already be for sale.
