articles.title: Cisco reports strong fiscal 2027 start driven by AI systems demand
articles.content:
Cisco Systems reported a 24% revenue increase for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, fueled by significant demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure and networking solutions, based on information published by CRN.

Chief Executive Officer Chuck Robbins highlighted a multi-billion-dollar networking super cycle as a primary driver for the company's growth. During the first quarter, networking revenue surged 43% to $11.13 billion, marking the ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth for the firm. Cisco now projects that AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers will reach $9 billion in fiscal 2027, representing 12% of total revenue.

The company reported total quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion, with non-GAAP earnings per share rising 40% to $1.40. Security segment sales also saw a 7% increase, reaching $2.12 billion, supported by the integration of Splunk and the recent acquisition of WideField Security. While product revenue grew by 42.6%, service revenue experienced a 7.1% decline.

Cisco leadership emphasized that customers are increasingly prioritizing integrated networking and security architectures to manage the complexities of the agentic AI era. These financial results represent the strongest growth rates for the company in over 15 years, reflecting a broad-based expansion across all major product families.

Source: CRN

articles.title: Trump-Ordered Vaccine Safety Report Delayed Past Deadline
articles.content:
A report on the safety of childhood vaccines is delayed, the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said.

“It’s still going through the clearance process,” Dr. Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, said in Washington during an event held by the Milken Institute on Nov. 12.

Schwartz described the plans as a report and acknowledged that the Nov. 8 deadline has passed. She declined to provide any details from the report, saying reporters should ask National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, who is leading the task force.

The agency did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

The report is designed to be given to the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel, known as ACIP, according to Schwartz.

“ACIP will be able to take that report, decide whether there is merit to some of the things in the report or not,” she said. “But that is the goal.”

Health officials in October said they’re accepting nominations for new members for the panel.

“Nominees will be selected to represent a balanced range of scientific, clinical, and public health expertise relevant to the Committee’s mission, including person(s) knowledgeable about consumer perspectives and/or social and community aspects of immunization programs,” the notice reads.

“We’re still waiting to hear from the appellate court about the case,” Schwartz said on Thursday.

She added later: “As soon as we know whether we can actually reconstitute ACIP, we will do so. We’re just putting out the notice so that when the appellate court, if the appellate court rules in our favor, we’ll be ready to go, hit the ground running.”

A designated federal official, who was not identified, will decide which applicants will become ACIP members, despite the ACIP charter saying the health secretary shall select new members, the CDC director said.

She also said that nine individuals whom Kennedy appointed are also being asked whether they want to stay on.

Measles

The Pan American Health Organization is meeting this week to decide whether the United States will lose its measles elimination status or whether a chain of transmission involving a certain measles strain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months. There have been more than 5,100 measles cases recorded in the country in 2026, the highest annual number since 1991.

Regardless of what the organization decides, the CDC will continue supporting states with vaccines, personnel, and other support, Schwartz said.

She and Kennedy have both endorsed the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine as the best way to prevent measles. But many of the cases are occurring among communities that include unvaccinated people, according to the CDC and states.

“Having big CDC come in and say ‘Verily, thou shalt’ is not going to work,” Schwartz said.

“But what will work is going with the states, with those trusted agencies, to talk about what can we do to bring awareness to these close-knit communities.

“Because once again, these communities typically do not believe in the MMR vaccine; they don’t believe in vaccinations in general. Some of them can be convinced. Some of them can’t be convinced. So it’s really sort of a different way of thinking about it.”

If people cannot be convinced to get a vaccine, they should be told about the seriousness of measles, how to identify the disease, when to see a doctor, and how to isolate to avoid infecting relatives, the CDC director said.

Conversations With Kennedy

Schwartz, a former military health officer who was confirmed in August, indicated in her confirmation hearing that she goes over areas of disagreement with superiors in private. She said that has happened with Kennedy, including during the daily meetings she and other division heads have with the health secretary.

“We have robust conversations. What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He’s not someone who just says, ‘No, I don’t have room for that.’ He really does value different opinions,” Schwartz said.

Kennedy’s leadership style is inclusive and decisive, often involving holding a meeting with people, hearing their opinions, and making a decision, according to Schwartz. She said her style is more insular and indecisive.

Sometimes, Kennedy’s decisions have been in her favor; sometimes, they have been against her.

Schwartz also said she has never met with new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, whom Kennedy recently praised, and that she is prepared to work with incoming lawmakers, including the Democratic doctors and public health experts who helped flip the House of Representatives and Senate.

“We may not agree on every issue,” she said, “but I do think there’s a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again.”

articles.title: Trace3 completes acquisition of Calian Group U.S. IT business
articles.content:
Trace3 has finalized its acquisition of the U.S. commercial information technology assets of the Canada-based Calian Group, a move designed to bolster the firm's geographic reach and technical capabilities, based on information published by CRN.

The transaction, which was initially announced in August, involved an upfront cash payment of $31 million and the assumption of approximately $12 million in net liabilities. Through this deal, the Irvine, California-based company adds 140 employees, two network operations centers and its first security operations center. Chief Executive Officer Joe Quaglia stated that the acquisition provides significant expansion in Texas and Minnesota, two regions that align with the company's central go-to-market strategy.

The integration brings new talent into the organization, including former Calian executives Christopher Farah and Christopher Grammer. Beyond geographic growth, the addition of a security operations center enhances the firm's ability to address emerging threats, particularly as enterprise clients navigate risks associated with autonomous artificial intelligence.

Quaglia noted that there is minimal overlap between the existing client bases, offering an opportunity to introduce the company's value proposition to a new set of customers. The firm plans to continue pursuing strategic acquisitions to expand its service portfolio and market presence.

Source: CRN

articles.title: Who gets the final say over your health?
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | iHeartRadio | Podcast Index | RSS

Who gets the final say over your health? In this episode of The Nurses Report, Ashley Caputo, RN, FMP, examines healthcare headlines through a Christian, conservative, holistic lens, connecting government decisions with the choices families face in hospitals, pharmacies, and their own homes.

With Veterans Day this week, Ashley begins with the promises America owes those who served. The discussion explores VA research involving MDMA and psilocybin, recent claims-processing announcements, and the difference between documenting toxic exposure and receiving a medical evaluation. Veterans and their families deserve clear explanations, meaningful follow-up, and practical help accessing the benefits they earned. Honoring their service should extend far beyond a holiday acknowledgment.

California’s new supplement restrictions raise another question about authority and access. AB 2030 restricts sales to minors of certain products marketed for weight loss or muscle building, with creatine among the ingredients courts may consider. Ashley examines the role of product marketing, retailer presentation, parental responsibility, and the consequences of broad restrictions on supplements.

The episode also examines FDA approval of Moderna’s mRNA influenza vaccine, MFLUSIVA, for adults fifty and older, including accelerated approval for the indication in adults sixty-five and older. Ashley explains why knowing the actual product matters and why an announcement about reduced federal mRNA research funding does not mean every mRNA product or development program has stopped. Patients deserve specific information before making a decision.

At the center of the conversation is informed consent, including informed refusal. When a patient declines a recommended scan or treatment, was the reason for the recommendation explained? Did the patient understand what might be missed, what alternatives were available, and what could happen without further evaluation? Ashley argues that meaningful education must support both agreement and refusal. A documented “no” does not, by itself, tell us what the patient understood.

Drawing on verified legal examples, the discussion separates informed-consent claims from other medical-negligence theories while keeping the patient’s experience central. Ashley also examines Chiles v. Salazar and the Supreme Court’s treatment of government restrictions on a licensed counselor’s speech, highlighting questions about conscience, religious liberty, and the freedom to seek guidance consistent with personal convictions.

Additional stories include proposed changes affecting compounded peptides, revised hormone-therapy warnings, research connecting certain PFAS exposures with estrogen receptor-negative breast cancer, and efforts to modernize prior authorization. Each raises practical questions about transparency, access, accountability, and whether healthcare decisions reflect the needs of the individual.

Throughout the episode, Ashley calls for a healthcare culture that welcomes questions, respects parental involvement, considers environmental and lifestyle factors, and treats patients as active participants. Government announcements and institutional policies should translate into understandable choices and measurable improvements for the people affected.

The episode closes with gratitude for veterans and their families and the reminder from Galatians 6:2 to bear one another’s burdens. Faith, advocacy, and personal responsibility belong in the conversation about caring for our neighbors. Listeners are encouraged to read beyond the headline, ask what a recommendation means for their circumstances, and keep their voice in the room.

  • https://www.dav.org/get-help-now/
  • https://www.legion.org/contact
  • https://nvlsp.org/services/
  • https://www.vfw.org/assistance/va-claims-separation-benefits

The Nurses Report on America Out Loud airs weekdays at 10 AM ET. Listen on iHeartRadio, our world-class media player, or our free apps on Apple, Android, or Alexa. All episodes of The Nurses Report on America Out Loud can be found on podcast networks worldwide, the day after airing on talk radio.

Transcript Summary of this podcast episode ⤵

A patient’s right to ask questions should not disappear at the hospital door. Neither should the responsibility of the people providing care to answer them. Healthcare loses its purpose when getting someone to comply matters more than helping that person understand.

Your body belongs to you. A professional title does not transfer ownership of your decisions to a clinician, an insurance company, or a government agency. Every person has God-given dignity, including the patient who hesitates, disagrees, or needs more time.

Informed consent must mean more than a signature. Before recommending a scan, medication, or procedure, we should explain what we suspect, what remains uncertain, what alternatives exist, and what could happen without treatment.

When someone says no, the conversation deserves attention. Is the concern cost? Radiation? A frightening experience? We cannot assume that declining a recommendation means understanding its consequences. Writing “patient refused” does not tell us whether anyone listened.

That same standard should guide decisions about vaccines, hormone therapy, supplements, and compounded treatments. Patients deserve clear explanations of risks, evidence, regulatory changes, and unanswered questions. Government agencies should explain restrictions. Clinicians should have room to discuss reasonable options and the responsibility to do so honestly.

For veterans, these principles carry particular weight. Faster claims processing and expanded facilities deserve recognition when they translate into accurate decisions and timely care. A completed form cannot tell us whether a veteran received an appointment, understood the next step, or finally felt heard.

Families should not have to prove their persistence while someone they love is suffering.

Honoring service requires sustained attention to the whole person: sleep, pain, mental health, relationships, faith, and purpose. Our gratitude must reach beyond a holiday meal or patriotic message.

We fulfill that obligation by listening, explaining, advocating, and helping carry one another’s burdens throughout the year, every year.

Welcome to the hotel. Take a deep breath. Take the higher roll. Set the other way.

They will take it from me. Welcome back to the Nurses Report on America Out Loud. I’m your host, Ashley Caputo, registered nurse and functional medicine practitioner. And today we’re going to do something a little different.

We’re opening up the healthcare headlines and looking at the decisions being made in our courtrooms, our government agencies, pharmacies, hospitals, and insurance offices that can affect your family before you even hear about them. So some of these stories maybe deserve some applause, and some deserve a much closer look. But all of them deserve more than a headline and instruction to stop asking questions. So we’re going to be talking about California putting age restriction on certain supplements.

We’re talking about an mRNA flu vaccine that has already received FDA approval. We’re going to be talking about change, changes involving peptides, hormone therapy, and what a licensed counselor is allowed to say. And we’re spending some time on something that matters deeply to me as a nurse and as a patient advocate. Informed consent, including what happens when a patient says no.

Because if the system only respects your decision when you make the decision that it wants, we have a problem. And since today is Veterans Day Week, we are also looking at what’s happening for veterans. My husband is an Army veteran. So this isn’t just some distant policy discussion.

These are real people, real families and promises made to people who served this country and who are still serving this country. I want to begin with a principle that runs through everything we’re discussing today. Your body belongs to you, your consciousness belongs to you. Your responsibility to steward your health doesn’t disappear when you walk into a hospital.

And it doesn’t transfer to a government agency because someone has a title. And as a Christian, I believe every person has God-given dignity. That dignity doesn’t depend on whether you understand medical terminology, whether you have good insurance, whether you agree with a recommendation, or whether you are easy to fit into a 15-minute appointment. As a nurse, I believe education is a part of care.

As someone who approaches health through a functional and holistic lens, I want us asking what is contributing to illness? What’s the root cause? What can be addressed? And how do we support the whole person?

And as a conservative, I want the government to explain why it needs more authority before it takes more authority. So that’s what we’re going to be diving into today. So before we talk about like supplements and court decisions, let’s talk about the people that we are honoring this week. So, first, on November 10th, the White House issued its Veterans Day proclamation.

The administration reported processing a record of 3.1 million disability claims this year, reducing the claims backlog by more than 70% during president’s second term, and opening 47 new healthcare facilities. So separately, the VA announced in late October that it’s hiring more than 2,000 additional employees to process rising claims. I have seen veterans waiting for their claims to be processed, and it is a grueling process. I lived it with my husband.

For years we fought to get his benefits processed and finally got him service connected. So I applaud this. If those changes mean that veterans get accurate decisions and timely care, I think that’s totally worth recognizing. I want the improvements to succeed.

I want the administration to keep the promises it makes to veterans. But and this is a big but we have to measure the success from the veteran side of the desk as well. Did the right records get reviewed? Was the decision accurate?

Just because something got processed doesn’t mean that it was processed right. Can the veteran get an appointment? Great, you have benefits. Can you actually see somebody?

When a specialist recommends something, can they actually receive it? Does the spouse understand what’s going on and what’s happening? Or is the family left just calling different departments and each department says it’s someone else’s responsibility? If you’ve ever called the VA, what I’m talking about.

We can celebrate an improvement and still insist on accountability and transparency. All of those things belong together. And I do want to say for the veteran listening who is just exhausted by paperwork, because I get it. I know I have I have walked with many veterans through this process.

I have walked with my husband through this process. And I want to say this clearly: needing help navigating your care does not make you weak. There is nothing honorable about making a sick person prove how persistent they can be. So ask for the help, ask for the guidance.

There are organizations out there that will help you, and I will try to post some of those in the show notes. But there’s also another veteran story this year that a lot of people may have not heard about. The VA is studying treatments that would have sounded very unlikely, I think, in a federal healthcare announcement just even a few years ago. So in May, the VA announced a randomized trial of MDMA assisted therapy for veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder.

In August, it announced Pivot, a trial studying cyclocybin for treatment-resistant major depression, including veterans who also have PTSD. These are clinical research programs with psychological support and, of course, controlled conditions. They’re not just, general VA prescription benefits. We also don’t know the outcome of how these trials are going, like what’s the positive, the negative, and what it looks like going forward.

But this is a significant development. It means, the conversation is expanding beyond simply asking whether someone has tried another antidepressant, because that’s typically what the VA does when they’re treating PTSD. They put you on antidepressant, anti-anxiety, and then they get you into group therapy and one-on-one therapy, which I’m okay with the therapy, but we can’t just throw medications at everybody. There is a lot of treatment out there.

The VA as bad of a rap as it gets, I’ve worked there. I’ve worked, I did cardiac step down most of the time, but I did do about a year, year and a half in the mental health side and worked in an inpatient facility. And we do a lot of good work, but there is so much room for improvement. And I also want room for thoughtful research.

And veterans should be treated as people who deserve the full picture, right? We need to know what’s known, what’s still being studied, what are the risks. If you participate in this study, like what’s involved and also what happens afterwards. The whole person needs to matter, right?

Not just their mental health symptoms, but their sleep, their pain, their physical health, their marriage, their sense of purpose, their ability to function, their faith, their connection to people. A veteran should never feel that the only acceptable goal is just becoming quiet enough that nobody has to ask how you’re really doing. Now, there’s another distinction that’s especially relevant to a functional conversation. And I was somewhat excited to hear about this, but then very much disappointed.

But it’s toxic exposure screening. So the VA says veterans who meet the basic service and discharge requirements and had qualifying toxic or other hazardous exposures may be eligible to enroll in healthcare without first applying for disability benefits. So typically, to get services and to get health care, you have to be service connected, meaning you’ve applied for benefits and been approved. Something that’s wrong with you is service connected to the VA. And then there’s different percentages, and depending on what percentage is how much access you have.

So, enrolled veterans, they’re offered an initial toxic exposure screening and follow-up at least every five years. But listen carefully to what the screening actually is. The VA describes it as a brief conversation about possible exposures. You heard me right.

It’s a brief conversation about possible exposures. Its provider guidance explicitly says it’s not medical screening for a disease and it’s not part of the disability benefits claim process. And that distinction is very important. Answering questions about burn pits, contaminated water, chemicals, or other exposures, I guess that’s a starting point.

But it should lead to a conversation about what comes next when a veteran has health concerns. If you thought checking that box meant someone tested your body for exposure-related illness, you could walk away with a very different understanding from what actually happened. So you have to ask what was documented, what follow-up is being offered, do my symptoms need a separate evaluation? Does a benefit claim require a separate application?

Who can help me connect those pieces? Those are reasonable questions and they deserve clear answers. For me, honoring veteran veterans means that, I mean, we just we don’t stop at posting some patriotic graphic and a restaurant discount. While I think it’s nice and I’m not against those things, our veterans very much appreciate what happens on Veterans Day when they’re able to go out and get a meal.

When I worked with the homeless veteran population, this day was very exciting. They got to go to restaurants that they never got to go to, and they got to sit down and have a meal. So I very much approve. But this is not where it should stop, and it shouldn’t just happen one day a year.

We listen, we help families understand the next steps. We need to make sure an administrative process doesn’t become the final destination for a person who needs care. It’s very frustrating, and I’ve seen the fallout that happens when veterans get pushed over the edge. I have worked at the VA when a veteran walks onto campus in full head-to-toe military gear and sits down on a bench and takes his own life with a bullet.

I have been on campus when a bomb has been planted at the benefits department and the entire place shuts down, not knowing if I was going to be able to get safely home to my children. I’ve held veterans’ hands while they cry. I’ve taken care of the homeless veterans who have nowhere to go and no one’s ever listened to them or acknowledged that they need help. I’ve been there.

So to every veteran listening and every spouse who has spent hours organizing records and pushing for answers, I want to tell you thank you. Your service and your family’s sacrifice deserve more than just one day of recognition. Now, switching gears a little bit, let’s move from federal veterans policy to California. I know that’s a big jump, but in California, certain supplement purchases are about to come with age restriction.

Governor Gavin Newsom, he signed Assembly Bill 2030, and this was signed back in September. And beginning January 1st, 2027, the law restricts sales to people under 18 of dietary supplements marketed or otherwise represented for weight loss or muscle building, along with over-the-counter diet pills. There is a prescription exception, but creatine is specifically named among ingredients a court may consider when deciding whether a supplement falls within the law. So when you hear, California banned creatine for minors, understand there’s a scope here, right?

The law doesn’t prohibit every product merely because it contains creatine. The product’s claims and how it is represented, that matters. And I think that that’s a problem as well. So that leads this conversation becomes important because this is bigger than just a supplement, right?

So courts I this makes it hard on the real retailer and small business, is is how I see this. I don’t see this as helping the population, but I just see this as like a hurdle for businesses. But anyway, the court can consider the way the retailer labels, groups, categorizes, or displays the product. And the restriction can reach beyond the words printed by the manufacturer.

So think about that as a parent. You’re trying to understand what is appropriate for your own teenager, and now the store also has to work out whether the way it’s represented or the way it presents a product brings it under the restriction. And you can face fines. My concern is the reach of the rule and the precedent behind it.

When the government puts a broad category of products behind an age gate, I want to know exactly what the problem is solving, right? What evidence supports the boundaries and what happens to families whose circumstances maybe don’t fit the broad category? And if a company is making false claims, we need to address the false claims. If a product is adulterated, address the adulteration.

If advertising is manipulative, identify the conduct and address it directly. I want a clear explanation for why restricting access across a category is an appropriate response. And then there’s also the practical question that I brought up before. And it’s for small businesses.

How do they make these decisions? Who helps them interpret the rule? If they’re worried about a penalty, will they simply just restrict more products? They won’t sell them, they won’t, they won’t have the product.

And that’s a question about how a law operates in real life. It’s one thing to say it, to write it down on paper, but now it’s being implemented. The written intention and the checkout counter experience, those are two totally different things. And from a parent’s perspective, I want education that helps me evaluate a label.

I want clear ingredient information. I want honest claims and accountable companies. And I want to understand what my child’s using and why. I also want my role respected as a parent.

And from a broader healthcare perspective, like we got to have consistency. If the government says its priority is protecting young people, then the public should be able to ask how that principle is applied across the entire system. Why is my child allowed to walk into a gas station and buy an energy drink, but they can’t buy creatine? I care about children.

That’s why I care about evidence, proportionality, parental authority, and whether the law delivers what it promises. And I think the takeaway from the story is simple, right? So the California law is signed, its restrictions begin in January. The details are broader than just the headline, says if you’ve scrolled on social media, you might have seen creatine’s been, it’s not being sold to people under 18 and blah, blah, blah.

But it the law itself is a lot broader than that. And I think leaves room for a lot of questions. Like, basically, this law is putting pressure on small businesses to make decisions on how they promote the product. It’s more about marketing, I think, than anything else.

It’s not really looking at the safety of the children. So I want to know like, how does how does this help, right? Like, like, what are we actually doing here? I think we could probably focus on other things that would help overall health than this, but not that I want children going and having easy access to to dieting pills and things like that.

That’s not what I’m saying. But where does it end if we if we start here? And, how does this make sense over allowing them to buy junk food and monster drinks and and all of those things? So okay, before we go to break, let’s talk real quick about the mRNA flu vaccine and informed consent.

Because an mRNA flu vaccine has already received FDA approval in the United States. And we talked about this a little bit last week, but on August 5th, 2026, the FDA approved Moderna’s Mflusiva for adults 50 and older. And if you remember, we mentioned last week that the clinical trials showed that the people taking the mRNA influsiva had higher risk of adverse events and side effects than the other group. But safe and effective, right?

So the FDA identifies the product as an influenza vaccine, which it’s not really a vaccine, but using mRNA. So for adults 65 and older, the indication was granted through an accelerated approval. Where have we heard that before? The approval letter requires a study comparing it with a high-dose influenza vaccine.

The study completion listed for July 2029 and the final report due May 2030. Just in case it is 2026, just so . So we’ll have the results to the study in 2030. But it’s already been FDA approved for the public.

So when someone says it’s time for your flu vaccine, and if you’ve made the decision that you’re going to get the flu vaccine, which I don’t advocate for, I think you need education and informed, education to make an informed decision before getting the flu vaccine. But if that’s what you’ve chosen is right for you, you should be able to ask, what vaccine are you getting? What’s the product called? Can I see the package information?

What does the approval cover? Like the the approval of this mRNA vaccine, you need to understand, is this just being offered to everyone? Are you going to be given an option? Are there other products available?

What are the risks and uncertainties? Like this deserves a conversation, not just walking into a pharmacy and sitting down and getting a flu shot, and you get handed a piece of paper and you go on about your way. This deserves education and a conversation about what it is that’s actually being injected into your body. And we also have to talk about what this accelerated approval means.

It deserves an explanation. The FDA’s letter describes an approval pathway that can rely on an endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, with further study required to verify that benefit. In this instance, the older adult indication carries a required post-marketing study. What is post-marketing study?

That means it’s being studied after it’s been released to the public and being given to the public. So we’re the guinea pigs. The older population is the guinea pig in this instance. My point is that the patient should understand what is established, right?

Like you should know if you’re getting an mRNA vaccine and that it’s in post-marketing study and what the side effects and risks are. And you should know that in clinical trial, people did experience a higher rate of adverse events. And if we’re willing to give this to the public, we should be willing to withstand a patient reading the approval letter and having a conversation about it. If you, the healthcare professional administering this flu vaccine, just know for certain that it’s safe, that it’s effective, and that there’s no concern and about the vaccine and what their risks are, you should be able to have a conversation with them about it.

Now, there’s a second piece to the story because some people heard that the administration was pulling back on mRNA technology and assumed that that meant the technology was maybe disappearing a little bit. But in August 2025, the HHS announced a window of 22 Barta mRNA vaccine investments worth nearly $500 million. So it’s like they presented this to the public to appease everyone that, hey, look, we’re not funding research on mRNA technology anymore. But that was a funding decision involving a particular program.

The FDA approval of a product is totally different. So both are happening, right? They pulled back funding from some mRNA research, but they went ahead and approved FDA approved an mRNA vaccine. And they’re still researching.

So they only pulled funding for certain programs. So we need to not we don’t need to stop paying attention. We need to be diligent or diligent about looking into what’s actually going on. And I don’t think supporting an administration or not supporting an administration requires like surrendering your responsibility to examine its agency’s decisions, right?

Like we shouldn’t just be looking in and and under a microscope if it’s an administration that we don’t like because we’re worried about what they’re gonna do. And vice versa, we shouldn’t like take off the gas pedal because we like the administration. We’re just gonna what, blindly trust what they’re doing? I don’t blindly trust any agency or politician.

So I think we should we should really be focusing on what they’re actually doing and not just what the headlines are saying. Because if you read the headline on mRNA funding, you thought that maybe they were just removing it, that they were stepping back. And that’s how they presented it because they know that that’s what their followers want. That’s what the public wants.

But instead, secretly, I guess not secretly, it’s out there, but they went ahead and approved this mRNA vaccine. And I just think that the person sitting in that pharmacy chair, you you walked into Walgreens or CVS or whatever, that person lives with the decision. So they deserve to have a conversation about what’s actually being administered to them. Because if they walk out and have an adverse reaction and it wasn’t true informed consent, is that really the world that we want to live in?

I mean, that’s the world that we’re living in now, right? We were all, or not all of us, but a lot of people took the COVID vaccine thinking that it’s safe and effective and that everything is gonna be fine. And now you’re dealing with people with long COVID, myocarditis, blood clots, people that didn’t make it, people that died. And this is all being tied back to this vaccine.

So, this post-marketing study, what it’s gonna tell us in the future how bad it is, I’m not okay with that. And I don’t think you should be either. We deserve better than that. So, but that’s what’s going on with that.

We have more to talk about on informed consent. So, when we get back from break, we’re gonna dive into that. So, stick with us. You’re listening to The Nurses Report on America Out Loud.

We’re gonna hear from our sponsors, and we’ll be back in a minute. Before the break, we were talking about, informed consent with this mRNA technology and the flu vaccine. But this brings me to another issue with informed consent, because it it goes broader than just getting a vaccine. Informed consent spans across all of healthcare. Everything that you do, every medication, treatment, procedure, all of it requires informed consent.

So what does it mean to make an informed medical decision? Think about this scenario, and it happened recently. A woman with abdominal pain and swelling kept seeking care. She kept going to the emergency room.

And then a CT scan was recommended, but she declined it. And later, she says that nobody explained to her why it mattered or what the doctors were concerned that they could miss. And I want to examine that a little bit from the patient’s side of the bed. Because as a nurse, it’s easy for me to understand why they would want a CT scan when you have abdominal pain and distension, right?

Makes sense. Makes sense to me. But I’m not trying to get another nurse or a doctor to agree to this procedure. We can’t assume that she understands what a CT scan is or why it would be needed and the importance of it.

So we need to know what she, what did she actually understand? Did she hear that the scan was one possible next step? Was it like, well, you could do this or you could do this? We can do the CT scan or you could go home and and monitor and see how how you’re doing?

Or did she understand that the clinician was worried about a potentially serious condition? Did anyone ask why? Why was she hesitant? Was she worried about the radiation, the contrast?

Maybe she’s claustrophobic, maybe she had a prior bad experience. Did she think being discharged just meant that there was no serious condition? I mean, those questions change the conversation. And there’s a difference between a person declining after meaningful explanation and a person declining an order that she doesn’t understand.

And there’s a difference between respecting a patient’s decision and deciding that a refusal ends your responsibility to communicate. And my position is very straightforward. A patient needs meaningful information, whether the eventual answer is yes or no. That’s not my job.

My job is to present you with all the information that you need to make an educated decision for yourself. And if you have hesitation or decline something I’m recommending, I also want to know why. So we can talk about that and make the best plan for you. Because when when someone’s declining something, I think that’s often the moment when the most important conversation needs to begin.

So there was a a woman who did go to the ER with these symptoms, and she did decline several times. She declined a CT scan. Did someone stop and say, here’s why we’re recommending this test. Here are reasonable alternatives.

Here is what we could miss if we don’t investigate further. And here’s what I recommend if you decide against it. Here’s what we’re trying to find out. This is what I’m worried about for you.

Because in the end, she came back and it turned out that she had a ruptured appendix and a bowel obstruction. She sued and lost because the courts decided that the burden of informed consent was not on the hospital, it was not on her providers. That she took responsibility because she declined the CT scan. So it’s her fault.

And I think they get it wrong because now I don’t know all the details of the case. And I wasn’t in the room, when they were talking to her. For all I know, one of the nurses like sat in there with her and really talked to her about it, and she just didn’t want to do it for whatever reason. I don’t know.

But she’s claiming that she didn’t understand how serious it could be if she didn’t do the scan and didn’t understand that this was actually needed to determine what was going on with her. I don’t know. But what I do know is that the decision of the court saying that the responsibility, the burden of informed consent is not on the providers unless consent’s actually given. That’s so backwards.

Because if you what informed consent means that you have all the education and information that you need to consent. That should be what you get to be able to make the decision for yourself. So I don’t really understand, but there’s actually been other cases like this, which is mind-blowing too. So there are court decisions that show why this legal framework, I mean, it matters because so there’s an older case that was in Maryland.

It’s Landon V. Zorn. And it involved a man who declined a recommended CT scan and later argued that he had not been told the risks of declining. Now, this was this lady’s same argument here. So this was back in 2005, and Maryland’s highest court upheld the refusal to give the requested informed consent jury instruction.

Its reasoning included the absence of affirmative invasion of bodily integrity and the plaintiff’s failure to provide expert testimony establishing the asserted disclosure duty under the professional standard of care. There’s a lot of legal mumbo jumbo, but and every state, I guess, treats this informed, they call it informed refusal. So meaning that you should have known enough to make a good decision for yourself and the burdens not on the provider, is basically what it’s saying. And not every state treats informed refusal the same way.

So, but it gives us, this important question to ask. Like when the law draws these lines, these categories, what happens to the patient saying, I couldn’t make an informed decision because I wasn’t given the information? That is never something I want to hear from my patient, that’s for sure. Now, California provides they have a different example, and this I think is more in line with the way that it should be.

Its civil jury instruction on informed refusal says a practitioner must explain important risks of declining a procedure in language the patient can understand. The instruction includes serious injury, death, and significant complications when relevant. I don’t even know how this is a question, right? Like, how can this even vary from state to state?

The concept itself makes sense. If a risk matters enough that a reasonable person would consider it when deciding, the patient needs to hear about it. You deserve to have the information and education that you need to make a decision for yourself. So you need to be told the meaningful risks of doing something, but you also need to be told the meaningful risks of declining.

Tell me what what you suspect, what remains uncertain. Tell me what information are you going to gather from this test? And then provide alternatives that are reasonable for my circumstances and the risks and benefits of those. And then you have to respect the decision.

And it all should be documented. Everything should be documented, not just patient refused. That’s not good documentation. Patient refused, education provided, blah, blah, blah.

Like the whole conversation should be documented. You can put quotations in there, exactly what the patient said, exactly what you told the patient. This is not a one-sentence conversation. Hey, doc ordered a CT scan.

I just need you to sign this consent. No, I don’t want a CT scan. Okay. Patient refused.

That shouldn’t be the end of the discussion. That shouldn’t have been how any of that goes. And I don’t know exactly how it went down. So I’m just generalizing here.

But I think it’s really important, when people do have concerns about a procedure, a person worried about, radiation, they’re entitled to ask thoughtful questions and have a conversation. A per a person that’s worried about contrast, maybe they have, have had kidney issues in the past and they’re worried about the contrast, they’re entitled to ask, why is it being recommended? And what alternatives do I have? A person who’s self-pay, who cannot afford the bill, is entitled to ask.

These concerns should be addressed. It’s just a part of care. And I have, I have a huge problem with health care culture that spends pages documenting a patient’s refusal while offering very little evidence of an effort to understand it and educate. I want the documentation to reflect an honest conversation.

And a prior discharge should never become reason to stop listening. So if you see that someone’s refused care or left AMA, that should not change how you’re approaching the situation. All of this, this isn’t patients being difficult. It’s participating in your care.

And for my fellow nurses and clinicians listening, think about the position you occupy. You may be the person who realizes the patient has misunderstood something everyone else assumed was clear. You may be the one who hears the financial concern or the fear from a previous hospitalization. That’s the opportunity to advocate.

Sometimes the most useful thing that we can say is before this patient makes a final decision, we need to clarify what they understand. I want a system where that’s supported, where a nurse has time to raise a concern and where the response is curiosity and care. And as a Christian, I also think about the obligation to tell the truth in a way another person can actually receive. Expertise is a responsibility.

Your role as a nurse, as a doctor, as a provider is a responsibility. If someone’s relying on your knowledge, there should be humility in the way that you explain it. And that’s the standard that I’m arguing for. Okay, so let’s now talk about the Supreme Court decision that raises another question about the relationship between government authority and the healthcare encounter.

So on March 31st, 2026, the United States Supreme Court decided Child v. Salazar. The case concerned a Colorado counselor’s challenge to a state restriction on conversation therapy as applied to her talk therapy. The court held that the law in that application regulated speech based on a viewpoint, and that the lower courts had failed to apply sufficiently rigorous First Amendment scrutiny. That is the constitutional holding we’re discussing.

So this court wasn’t deciding whether a particular counseling approach produces a particular clinical result. The broader issue is whether a government can regulate what a licensed professional says based on which viewpoint the professional expresses. And as someone who cares about religious freedom and just medical freedom, I think that this deserves serious attention. People come to counseling with different convictions, different goals, different beliefs about their lives, and different reasons for seeking help.

And I want them to be able to ask questions and talk honestly about those convictions. I want a person with Christian beliefs to be able to seek counseling that takes those beliefs seriously. And I want a clinician to be able to have a respectful conversation without the government treating expression of disfavored viewpoint as the central offense. A license carries responsibilities.

It should not require a professional to pretend that conscious and constitutional rights no longer exist. For me, the patient remains central, right? What help is this person seeking? Are they being treated with dignity?

Are they being listened to? Is the conversation honest and voluntary? People deserve protection from coercion and abuse. They also deserve room to think, speak, and ask and seek guidance consistent with their convictions.

And I personally don’t want the government pre-selecting the only acceptable conclusion to a deeply personal conversation. And I don’t want professionals, associations or licensing systems functioning in a way that makes clinicians afraid to ask an honest question. The way we respond to disagreement matters. Can we have a conversation?

Can evidence be examined? Can a person express concerns without every disagreement immediately becoming a threat to their livelihood? That’s a serious issue across healthcare. The question of who may speak and understand what conditions affects what patients get to hear.

If we care about informed decisions, we should care about the conditions under which information and viewpoints can be discussed. I shouldn’t have to worry about my healthcare providers’ beliefs and convictions when I’m seeking care. We saw that happening when during the the run for presidency, and you had all these healthcare providers speaking out, nurses saying that they wouldn’t treat a Trump supporter or after the Charlie Kirk assassination, that they wouldn’t treat someone supporting him. They wouldn’t treat him if he had come into their ER.

It’s disgusting. As healthcare providers, we have a responsibility to treat everyone no matter what. I don’t care what your beliefs are. I mean, well, let me take that back.

I care because if it if it helps me provide care for you, if you’re a Christian and you want me to hold your hand and pray with you, that matters to me. But if you’re a non-believer and I’m a believer, that doesn’t matter to me. If you’re a liberal and I’m a conservative, doesn’t matter. I’m still gonna treat you as a person.

And when we’re talking about counseling and the government involvement and what counselors can say and how they can respond, I should be able to go see a counselor and speak freely about my convictions and my beliefs. If it’s a part of my therapy and I shouldn’t have someone else’s opinion being placed on mine. I should be supported in my convictions and my beliefs. Now, I think there’s a fine line, right?

Because if I believe that, it my beliefs are delusional and I need help that way, I want someone to be able to recognize that. But the government involvement in counseling such an intimate setting is really disturbing to me. So here’s another development I think that fits a conversation about access. On October 30th, HHS published a federal register notice announcing a draft enforcement discretion policy involving certain peptide ingredients used in patient-specific compounding.

So the draft describes an approach under which qualifying pharmacies and physicians could compound products using listed peptide substances while formal rulemaking proceeds. So it does not make those compounded products FDA approved, and a draft policy is not the same as a completed regulatory change. That distinction helps people understand the story without losing sight of why it matters. So for people interested in peptides, the practical question is whether this leads to a clearer and more workable route for access, through legitimate clinical care.

I want patients to be able to understand the route, like what’s being prescribed, why is it being considered, who’s making it and what standards apply, what evidence supports its use for the actual goal being discussed, and what follow-up is planned. You shouldn’t have to question the is this product a good product for me? I feel like, you’re getting, if you’re getting it from a compounding pharmacy, you should be able to trust the quality of the product. And if it’s a doctor’s decision that this product is good for you, I think the government should butt out, honestly.

We compound a lot of things, and compounding pharmacies are used in functional medicine a lot because a lot of the things that you prescribe for people are not just readily available from your average pharmacy. And then when we’re talking about peptides, peptides are huge and they can be super beneficial. But I do agree that peptides should be you should work one-on-one with a provider to find what peptides are best for you. I don’t think it should be a free-for-all.

But, I also want regulatory decisions to just be explained in a way that respects people who are looking for these answers. Like if access is restricted, tell the public the specific reason. Is it because pharmaceutical companies, are wanting to take control of certain peptides to make a profit? And so they’re limiting access to compounding pharmacies.

I don’t know. But if policy changes explain, they have to explain the evidence or the consideration that drove that change. We shouldn’t just have to accept, well, that’s the rule. What I mean?

Like we deserve an explanation. And then, especially for those of us who work in functional medicine and people that prefer a functional approach, let’s keep the individual person and the goal in view. What are we trying to improve? And access and discernment, I mean, those things belong together because I want people able to explore reasonable options with full access to the information.

I want functional providers and providers in general to be able to access what they feel is appropriate for their patients without being regulated so much by, just being told, well, you can’t have that. But why? Why is it being taken? Why is it being regulated?

Why is it being changed? There’s room for this conversation. There should be transparency. And so this is a story to follow as a draft policy and the formal process is developing.

So we’re gonna have to keep an eye on this and see what decisions in Washington are affecting what a patient and a practitioner are able to discuss and obtain. So that’s something we really need to keep an eye on. So we’ll be watching that. I’ll let if there’s updates.

Right now, it’s just like, providers are are not sure what it’s gonna look like for their practice, like what’s gonna change. Maybe you’re already prescribing peptides and you’re worried about the fact that they’re not gonna be available. Or maybe you’re hoping that the availability is gonna be better through compounding pharmacies. But, that’s that’s yet to be seen.

And so we’ll have to keep an eye on that development. But again, government involving itself in healthcare is just it’s a sticky situation. I guess there’s some good sometimes, but a lot of the times it just provides more hurdles for providers to jump through. So speaking of that, let’s let’s turn to women’s health.

So on October 30th, HHS announced FDA approval of revised labeling for three additional estradiol patches. The revisions removed cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia statements from boxed warning sections. Similar changes had been approved for six hormone therapy products in February. Risks are still described elsewhere in labeling, and the endometrial cancer boxed warning remains for systemic estrogen-only products.

And for women who have been trying to understand their options, I mean, this is significant, y’all. I and I want to discuss how healthcare communicates, like when its message changes, right? So we have for decades talked about how estrogen’s bad, it puts you at risk for cancer, and so many people haven’t had access to hormone replacement therapy. And then now all of a sudden that changes.

I feel like people are gonna be skeptical, right? So, how do we have this conversation? If a woman made a decision years ago based on a warning, and then she hears about this revision, I mean, what does somebody call her? The next appointment, your doctor’s like, oh, guess what?

How we told you how dangerous that was? Well, I changed my mind. It’s totally not true. And so now I’m gonna prescribe you this medication.

I mean, does she know does she really understand why the decision was reversed, why it should be safe now when for years you were told that it was dangerous? And and I think we have to make sure that the conversation is individualized. Hormone, hormone replacement therapy doesn’t have to be for everybody. Women deserve a discussion that is specific enough to be useful.

Like, I want to hear your actual story. What’s happening with your sleep? How do you feel? What symptoms are affecting your day?

What’s important to you? What’s your history? What are your preferences? Do you even want hormones?

Because if you don’t, then we’re we’re going down a different route. And have you had hormone testing? If you haven’t had something like a Dutch test, I think it’s inappropriate to really just start someone on hormone replacement therapy. But I also don’t want a woman dismissed with, well, you’re getting older.

And just think as though, that explains everything that you’re experience, experiencing, and then just the conversation closes. And I don’t want the answer to every concern to be another disconnected prescription without a broader look at your health. So we are, we are actually out of time, and there was a couple more things I wanted to wanted to talk about, but unfortunately, we’re not going to be able to get to them. So I did want to close this out for Veterans Day.

I just want to close with gratitude for men and women who served and for the families who have carried so much alongside them. May our gratitude be visible in the way we show up, listen, and advocate throughout the year, not just on one day. Galatians 6, 2 says, bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. And that’s a responsibility that we can live out in our homes, our churches, our communities, and the way we care for people who serve this nation.

So thank you for listening. I’m Ashley. This is the Nurses Report on America Out Loud. Keep asking questions, keep your voice in the room.

God bless you, and God bless our veterans.

articles.title: ConnectWise probes malicious manipulation of ScreenConnect extensions
articles.content:
ConnectWise is investigating reports that a threat actor is manipulating third-party extensions within ScreenConnect environments to execute malicious remote commands against end users, according to a recent report by Channeldive.

The company has disabled access to specific extensions across 400 partner environments as a precaution. Cybersecurity firm Huntress reported that attackers installed rogue ScreenConnect clients on 288 endpoints across 48 organizations to deploy a toolkit known as SCKit. This toolkit utilizes 16 files, including PowerShell and batch scripts, to facilitate a multistage infection process. The attacker leverages the ScreenConnect Run command to establish persistent remote access and potentially steal session cookies.

Researchers from Sophos and BlackPoint are also monitoring similar unauthorized deployments. BlackPoint noted that the activity may involve a vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-84869, which the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added to its known exploited vulnerabilities catalog in September. ConnectWise has urged partners to disable third-party extensions, revoke active sessions, and implement multifactor authentication to secure their environments.

The company emphasized that on-premises partners must manually disable these extensions, as the provider cannot take unilateral action for those specific installations. Industry experts continue to analyze the scope of this campaign to determine if the identified vulnerability was the primary entry point for the attackers.

Source: Channeldive

articles.title: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach
articles.content:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights: 

Ex-FBI agent’s $2.47M crypto theft compromised bureau investigations

Patrick Steven Yaroch, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, faces up to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to wire fraud and money laundering over the theft of roughly $2.47 million in cryptocurrency. Yaroch used wallet credentials stored on FBI systems to make about 100 fraudulent transfers tied to 35 investigations. He took funds from investigation subjects and adversarial nation-state actors, and the thefts compromised multiple investigations and FBI sources and methods.

Baker Tilly client data taken from supplier’s platform

US accounting giant Baker Tilly is informing clients that hackers stole personal information, including Social Security numbers, from a platform operated by one of its service providers. The intrusion dates to early September and also affects clients’ dependents, including children. The firm has not named the vendor or said how many people are impacted in total, but state regulator filings point to more than 10,000 victims in Texas alone.

OpenAI agents concealed unauthorized activity

OpenAI has revealed new details about a July incident in which five AI agents conducting cybersecurity evaluations gained root privileges in CI workloads on the company’s research clusters. The agents used credentials and scripts left by earlier agents to modify evaluation settings, repair broken targets, and access restricted information. Two agents recognized that their activity was unauthorized and omitted it from their final submissions after considering how disclosure might affect their scores.

Prompt injection chain could have backdoored OpenAI’s Codex npm package

Depi researchers have described an attack chain against OpenAI’s Codex repository that started with a prompt injection in a GitHub Actions workflow and could have led to a malicious Codex release on npm. The issue-labeling workflow passed the title and body of any new issue to the Codex agent, so an attacker could execute code in the agent’s sandbox, read tokens from a GitHub runner process’s memory via .NET debug pipes, and poison the cache of a workflow with write permissions. The final step relied on a maintainer deleting a rogue release, which would yield a token trusted by npm. OpenAI has fixed the issue and awarded an initial $1,000 bounty.

Siemens details security advisory policy and planned improvements

Siemens has published a policy document that sets out how its PSIRT deals with product vulnerabilities and what its security advisories contain. Planned improvements include an API for automated lookups of product and vulnerability data, wider coverage of flaws in third-party components, more explicit “not affected” declarations, and getting advisory data into commonly used third-party vulnerability databases.

VulnCheck: Glasswing fixes lag far behind findings

VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity says that seven months after Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, he has tracked 442 CVEs credited to the company (about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year), only two of which are known to have been exploited in the wild. Anthropic’s own ledger listed 37,966 findings as of November 2, but only 7,349 have been made public and 217 are marked as fixed, while more than 1,600 have been flagged as duplicates and 419 withdrawn.

Railway puts unauthorized spend from stolen AI keys at $740,000

Railway has released a detailed incident report on the October attack, in which a threat actor used an undiscovered flaw in its build infrastructure to partially escape isolation, obtained a copy of the company’s code repository, and then abused a misconfigured OIDC binding to reach credentials that let it decrypt customer environment variables. At most 1.85% of workspaces (roughly 100,000) could have had variables decrypted. Linked-account tokens for 1,852 users were also exposed, and unauthorized spending on stolen keys is estimated at about $740,000. Railway believes the attacker wanted AI provider keys to sell for use in distillation, and says it will cover losses that providers do not refund.

Exposed MS SQL servers hijacked to deliver cryptominer and Gh0st RAT

Fortinet has analyzed a campaign in which Go-based malware with the open source Naabu scanner built in looks for internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances, and a companion tool then brute-forces logins using a list of more than 2,700 passwords. After a successful login, T-SQL commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or drop a loader, which installs a Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge update and a Gh0st RAT variant whose features include keylogging and data theft.

Microsoft urges weight audits after ‘Lazarus’ dormant neuron backdoor research

Microsoft researchers have described Lazarus, a technique that backdoors an LLM without any training by rewriting the weights of fewer than 10 dormant neurons, so that an agent built on the model behaves normally until a trigger (such as a date or an error message) makes it emit an attacker’s command. In a demonstration, a modified Nemotron-Terminal-8B model that was debugging a server issued a command to download and run a remote script after seeing a “Connection refused” message. Because the attack needs write access to the weights and can only be reliably detected by comparing them with the originals, Microsoft recommends verifying model provenance and auditing weights the way code is audited.

Connected cars exposed by flaws in automakers’ ForgeRock deployments

Researchers Sam Curry and Shubham Shah have disclosed weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity deployments of unnamed automakers that allowed them to take over customer accounts and send remote commands to connected vehicles, including unlocking doors and starting engines. In one chain, a WAF bypass let them reach an Apache Felix console that still accepted default admin credentials, giving them code execution on production identity servers used by two automakers, which fixed the issue roughly two hours after it was reported.

Palantir CISO LoSapio nominated to fill long-vacant CISA director post

President Donald Trump has nominated Michael LoSapio, Palantir’s CISO since September 2024, to lead CISA, which has not had a Senate-confirmed director since Jen Easterly left in January 2025, Nextgov reports. Should the Senate fail to act before this Congress adjourns, Trump would need to renominate him under an incoming Democratic majority whose members have questioned Palantir’s government work. Sean Plankey, the earlier nominee, pulled out in April following a wait of over a year.

Vanderbilt tells campus to power down devices amid attack claimed by BYOD group

US-based Vanderbilt University this week told everyone in its community to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi as its IT team worked on an active cybersecurity incident that it said could affect devices, systems and cloud-based services. The BYOD group has taken credit for the attack.

Related: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days

Related: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak

articles.title: Microsoft works to resolve widespread service outages
articles.content:
Microsoft is working to mitigate a widespread outage impacting its Microsoft 365 suite, including Teams, Exchange Online and Copilot, as first reported by CRN.

The Redmond, Washington-based vendor reported that the service disruptions were caused by a subset of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable, which strained the remaining infrastructure. Microsoft confirmed that the elevated load was not driven by an increase in user traffic. To address the issue, the company paused all deployments, moved traffic off affected infrastructure, and restarted servers to restore functionality. The outage impacted various services, including SharePoint Online, Microsoft Defender XDR, Outlook.com, and OneDrive.

Downdetector recorded significant spikes in user reports, with Outlook peaking at 130,000 reports and the Microsoft 365 suite reaching 46,000 reports. Industry partners noted that while cloud-hosted platforms are not immune to issues, the scale of this disruption during prime business hours highlights the critical need for robust redundancy and failover systems. Microsoft continues to redistribute connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure to balance the load and restore full service to all affected regions.

Source: CRN

articles.title: Microsoft 365 recovery advances as security and compliance disruptions persist
articles.content:
A Microsoft 365 outage can do more than interrupt a customer’s email. When the disruption reaches security portals, compliance tools and the services behind everyday response workflows, MSSPs have to figure out how it is affecting their ability to protect clients.

A widespread Microsoft 365 outage that began Thursday, Nov. 12, continued into Friday morning, interrupting functions across Microsoft’s collaboration, management and security services. Microsoft reported progress restoring service, but the incident remained unresolved in its 7:18 a.m. Eastern update.

For managed security providers, the challenge extends beyond helping customers regain access. Teams also need to assess which security functions are available, where visibility may be limited and whether established communication channels still work.

Disruption reaches security and compliance tools

Microsoft is tracking the broad incident as MO1550821. Its impact descriptions include problems accessing Defender interfaces and Purview functions, along with delays or failures involving some policy-dependent security experiences.

Other affected functions span Exchange Online, Copilot, Microsoft Graph and Intune, among additional services. Mailbox access through Outlook’s web, desktop and mobile connection methods may be interrupted, and email delivery may be delayed.

Those are dependencies that matter to MSSPs; an unavailable portal can complicate an analyst’s work, while delayed email can interfere with customer notifications and incident coordination. Providers need to determine the actual effect on each client’s environment rather than assume every affected service has stopped working entirely.

Microsoft says most core Teams calling, meetings and messaging remain functional, while Exchange-dependent calendar and scheduling functions can fail. Direct access to files stored in SharePoint Online also remains available, although some sharing and dependent features may experience problems.

A global outage with an uneven recovery

BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft listed the broad incident’s start at 1:26 p.m. Eastern Thursday, although the company had begun investigating Exchange Online connectivity problems earlier. Initially centered on the Americas, the potential impact expanded to users in any region.

Reuters reported that Outlook complaints on Downdetector peaked at 138,058 around 1 p.m. Eastern Thursday. Those reports indicate the scale of user complaints, rather than a complete count of affected customers.

“We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters.

Microsoft initially identified elevated infrastructure load, then explained that unexpectedly unavailable servers were straining the infrastructure that remained online. Its response included pausing deployments, redistributing traffic and restarting affected servers.

Later, Microsoft identified an overwhelmed process responsible for establishing secure connections that caused affected servers to stop processing requests, according to ABC’s coverage. Overnight adjustments produced partial recovery, but improvements did not consistently hold.

CIO reported that subsequent recovery changes were “not taking as expected,” with Microsoft adding virtual machine capacity and addressing traffic imbalances as it continued investigating.

Improvement does not mean an all-clear

Friday brought more encouraging updates. The Microsoft 365 Status account on X reported “early stabilization and capacity improvements,” while another update cautioned that “service health remains variable,” according to The Verge’s coverage of the posts. Microsoft also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help preserve delayed messages.

By 7:18 a.m. Eastern, Microsoft reported improving availability and email delivery in Europe, comparatively greater stability in Japan and improvement in North America. Intermittent problems remained, with reducing email queues and backlogs still a priority.

For MSSPs, recovery verification needs to extend beyond whether Outlook opens. Teams should check the security interfaces, integrations and notification paths they rely on, along with customer-facing communication channels. One recovered function does not establish that the entire workflow is healthy.

Microsoft says it has no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident and plans to publish a post-incident report after mitigation.

A substantial incident, without a confirmed record

The combination of worldwide reach, multiple affected workloads and disruption continuing into a second day makes this a substantial Microsoft 365 incident. Calling it the largest or longest, however, would get ahead of the evidence.

A November 2024 outage involving Outlook and Teams still had lingering email problems after 24 hours, according to The Standard’s reporting at the time.

The current outage’s business consequences are already tangible. Reuters reported that Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings announcement because of the disruption. OpenAI and Anthropic also reported problems involving Microsoft-connected services, illustrating how the impact extends beyond Microsoft’s own applications.

What MSSPs should prioritize

The immediate task is to understand the operational gaps. Providers should assess access to security tools, confirm whether expected alerts and notifications are arriving and document any limitations affecting monitoring or response.

Customer updates should explain the verified impact, available alternatives and when the next update will arrive. If email is unreliable, an update sent only by email has an obvious delivery problem. Previously established phone, text or external status-page channels can help bridge that gap.

Analysts should also distinguish confirmed Microsoft service failures from unrelated security events. The outage provides useful troubleshooting context, but it should not become the default explanation for every unexpected error or missing notification. Check Microsoft’s service health page alongside evidence from the customer’s environment.

Once service stabilizes, providers should review which monitoring, escalation and customer communication processes were disrupted. Could analysts reach the tools they needed? Could customers reach the security team? Did the fallback procedures hold up?

A continuity plan earns its value when the usual tools are unavailable. This outage is giving MSSPs and their customers a practical test of how well theirs works.

Matt Whitlock is tech editor for MSSP Alert, bringing more than 25 years of technology industry experience and a practical perspective on the tools and trends shaping managed security services. A seasoned editor, podcast host and event moderator, he covers cybersecurity and emerging technologies with a focus on what they mean for service providers and their customers.
