articles.title: Microsoft Struggles to Restore Email and Other Services in a Global Outage
articles.content:
From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue.

Microsoft said the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements,” and that there was “incremental improvement in several workloads.” But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company’s services and anecdotal reports on social media.

Microsoft scrambles to recover services

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.”

The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”

A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control.

Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.

An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution.

“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote.

In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”

“Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.”

Governments, businesses from Japan to Australia affected

The British government said it is “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” are in place to minimize disruption.

British police forces said they’re unable to receive crime reports online and are urging people to call emergency responders to make any urgent reports.

The National Pharmacy Association said people could face delays getting their prescriptions because the outage is affecting the email systems of the state-run National Health Service. Hospitals urged patients to attend appointments as usual.

U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.

Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

“They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company could not receive updates from its U.S. customers throughout Outlook. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.

Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

The Philippines’ Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that officials were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

articles.title: Court Lets Florida Age Verification Demands on Meta Proceed
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

A Florida appeals court on has refused to stop the state attorney general’s lawsuit against Meta.

The lawsuit is the same one in which Attorney General James Uthmeier in October asked the court to make Meta implement age checks on all Floridian users.

The court of appeals was asked by Meta to quash the decision of a lower instance, Pasco County Circuit Judge Alicia Polk, who last year refused to dismiss the case in a brief order, finding that the complaint “sufficiently pleads the claims.”

Meta went to the appeals court to try and get the lawsuit dismissed, but the judges found that the question of “irreparable harm” was “dispositive” and that they therefore “do not reach the merits of the petition.”

In a footnote, the court said that nothing in its opinion should be taken as “in any way to constitute a comment on the merits of the Attorney General’s FDUTPA complaint or Meta’s claim of immunity from liability under section 230 or the First Amendment.”

The court did, however, address some of these issues, and ruled that Section 230 is a “limited statutory immunity” and “not absolute immunity from involvement in any type of lawsuit” – which means that a platform can be made to go through the whole legal process before this defense is tested.

As for the First Amendment, the court found that the lower instance judge’s decision “does not come close to infringing on Meta’s First Amendment rights” and that “none of Meta’s First Amendment rights have been altered” – since no injunction has been granted yet.

The court did quote a previous ruling that said First Amendment protections extend to “unnecessary litigation that chills speech” – and said that the burden of litigating was not enough to establish such a violation.

Meta argued that it has “the right to exercise editorial discretion over the third-party content provided on its platforms” and “the right to be free from government-compelled speech.”

In its petition, Meta said, “Just as Meta could not be held liable for alleged harm caused by a direct exercise of editorial discretion, Meta cannot be held liable for alleged harm caused by publication features that simply operationalize its editorial choices.”

The state of Florida said that its case is about Meta’s “own conduct” – namely, its design choices – and conceded that editorial control of third-party content is protected.

In October, Florida was asking the court to make Meta “Request proof of age for Instagram and Facebook accounts belonging to users that Meta’s systems know or predict to be under the age of 14, and mark for deletion the accounts of those who do not verify their age within 30 days.”

Another request was to “Treat users who Meta has reason to believe are under 14 or under 18 years of age as under those respective ages unless the users age verify.”

If Meta cannot implement these measures within 30 days, the giant was to “cease to allow any Young Users access to its Platforms in Florida until these measures are implemented.”

In order to sort teenagers from adults, Meta would have to check everyone. As Reclaim The Net noted at the time, “you cannot check teenagers without checking everyone.”

After the ruling, Florida Attorney General Uthmeier said, “Unlike other states, Florida isn’t going to sell out.”

Florida is going it alone in this lawsuit, and it is doing so in order to try and achieve something that goes even beyond the national settlement reached earlier this year.

That settlement already requires age "assurance" for every Facebook and Instagram user in the states that are part of it – but both sides in that case waived any right to call the requirement unconstitutional.

Meta is no free speech hero – the giant is perfectly willing to censor content and silence users, and has done so on a massive scale. But the questions it raised in this case are the right ones – and the fact that the court has not addressed them is worrying.

articles.title: RFK Jr. Announces Funding to Study Ibogaine Psychedelic Drug
articles.content:
The federal government is slated to invest millions to develop treatment with ibogaine, a psychedelic drug, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on Nov. 12.

The Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, part of Kennedy’s agency, is investing up to $4.9 million to lay the groundwork for regulatory and manufacturing needs for future ibogaine clinical trials, rather than directly funding trials.

Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company will work on laying the foundation for a domestically manufactured, single-molecule ibogaine product for future trials exploring whether ibogaine can treat post-traumatic stress disorder and other mental illnesses, officials said. Another company, Beond Inc., which has treated patients with ibogaine in Mexico, will provide the government with data, Kennedy told reporters during a briefing in Washington.

“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “So we’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”

Kennedy also said that the government will be funding a separate effort to investigate whether ibogaine can treat addiction. That funding will be announced before the end of the year, he said.

Dr. Al Bugazia, senior adviser for special projects at the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, said veterans and millions of other Americans suffering from serious mental illness deserve the best possible care.

“Reports of successful ibogaine treatments are too promising to ignore. We owe it to our heroes and every person struggling to ask the bold questions and deliver results in years, not decades. As long as people continue to struggle, doing anything less is not an option,” he said.

The initial funding commitments span five years and will not be renewed unless certain milestones are reached, officials said.

“Researchers must establish whether ibogaine can help patients, identify who might benefit, determine whether those benefits justify the risks,” Kennedy said. “They must also investigate how long any improvement lasts. We will judge this work by the quality of the evidence.”

Doug Collins, secretary of Veterans Affairs, appeared with Kennedy and said that it’s important to develop the best science that can be produced in the effort to develop new treatments for post-traumatic stress disorder.

After Trump signed the order earlier this year, the Food and Drug Administration said it would speed up the review of three psychedelic drugs and allow a clinical study of an ibogaine derivative to move forward. In October, regulators asked the public to provide comments, data, and other information to inform research on ibogaine, including dose selection.

“Patients facing serious conditions that have not responded to existing treatments deserve rigorous scientific investigation of promising new approaches,” Dr. Michael Davis, director of the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, said at the time.

“With ibogaine, there are important scientific questions as well as serious safety concerns. We are seeking high-quality data and input that can help inform clinical research while putting patient safety first.”

The National Institute of Mental Health also announced on Thursday that it will provide up to $20 million in funding to support research into rapid-acting psychotropic drugs such as ketamine and psilocybin.

Some of the money will likely go to establishing a center to coordinate data collected across studies on the drugs, Andrea Beckel-Mitchener, acting director of the institute, said at the briefing.

articles.title: Google pushes second Chrome update this week
articles.content:
On November 11, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.78 for Linux. It includes 83 security fixes, five of which are rated Critical—the highest severity level. This update came out only two days after the previous one.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability.

A use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability happens when software accesses memory after it has released that memory for reuse. The program still has a reference to the old location, but the original object is no longer valid, and something else may now occupy that space.

The leftover reference is called a “dangling pointer” and is caused by a mistake in managing how long an object remains available. One part of a program may release it while another still expects to use it. That can happen because of confused ownership, faulty error handling, or a timing issue between tasks running simultaneously.

The consequences range from crashes and corrupted data to information leaks and, in some cases, execution of attacker-controlled code. The dangerous possibility is that an attacker can influence what replaces the freed object, then trick the program into treating that replacement as legitimate data or instructions for what to do next.

That explains why UAF flaws can receive critical severity ratings. However, the label describes a class of memory-management bugs, not a guaranteed outcome: the actual impact depends on the affected component, how reliably an attacker can exploit the mistake, and the protections in place.

articles.title: Indonesia Vice President Resigns Amid Protests As Christians Report Police Intimidation In Churches (Worthy News In-Depth)
articles.content:
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent

JAKARTA, INDONESIA (Worthy News) – Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation amid a dispute over his academic qualifications, his political aide confirmed Wednesday, as violent protests and allegations of police intimidation heightened tensions in the world’s largest Muslim-majority nation.

Gibran, 39, the son of former President Joko Widodo, offered to step down after court rulings raised questions about his eligibility for the 2024 election and 120 lawmakers sought proceedings that could lead to his impeachment.

The political crisis coincided with demonstrations over rising living costs, stagnant wages, devastating forest fires and government accountability. In Yogyakarta, clashes between security forces and demonstrators led to 157 detentions, including 21 minors, authorities said.

However, Christians told Worthy News that police activity had extended beyond the streets, with officers entering churches and warning congregations against joining anti-government protests. Authorities described the visits as community outreach intended to promote security and religious harmony.

“It seems they want war against their own people. We are very worried that this could escalate further,” a church worker told Worthy News, referring to confrontations between security forces and protesters.

INDONESIA VICE PRESIDENT RESIGNS

The standoff came as Gibran submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto on Wednesday, according to his political aide, Budi Arie Setiadi. Two sources in Indonesia’s parliamentary upper house said he was expected to formally submit his resignation letter to the chamber Thursday, initiating the approval process and the selection of a replacement.

His decision followed rulings by Indonesia’s Constitutional Court and Supreme Court that raised serious questions about whether his overseas education documents met election requirements. The Constitutional Court found insufficient evidence of the required qualifications but said it could not itself remove him from office.

Lawmakers from eight political parties signed a petition challenging his eligibility to remain in office. The initiative included members of the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, or PDI-P, who sought to invoke parliament’s constitutional right to express an opinion.

Gibran, who became vice president in October 2024, had reportedly offered to resign during a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday. The president was said to have advised him to pursue legal avenues to defend his academic qualifications.

The controversy has also exposed tensions between Prabowo and Gibran’s father, widely known as Jokowi, whose political support helped Prabowo win the 2024 presidential election.

MILITARY MOBILIZATION HEIGHTENS TENSIONS

Political tensions intensified after Indonesia’s military announced the mobilization of nearly 21,000 personnel for security operations in Jakarta last week, following the detention of senior police officers accused of illegally wiretapping President Prabowo Subianto.

The operation involved troops already stationed in Jakarta, reinforcements from outside the capital and more than 13,000 personnel placed on standby at military bases.

Military officials described the mobilization as a precautionary measure to maintain national security and stability, while also citing preparations for military exercises. Authorities denied that the troops were being deployed to suppress anti-government demonstrations.

The wiretapping investigation led to the detention of three senior police officers, including former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who had served as presidential chief of staff. He was subsequently dismissed from that position.

The developments added to concerns about the role of security forces in Indonesia’s political life as the government faced mounting public dissatisfaction and tensions between competing political factions.

YOGYAKARTA PROTESTS TURN VIOLENT

In Yogyakarta, a major university and cultural center on the island of Java, about 430 kilometers (267 miles) southeast of Jakarta, hundreds of students and civil society activists gathered Tuesday, Indonesia’s National Heroes Day, to demand higher wages, improved environmental policies and an end to restrictions on rallies.

Protesters also called for the withdrawal of the controversial Jaga Warga neighborhood security initiative, which critics say has contributed to intimidation. Representatives met Yogyakarta Governor Sultan Hamengkubuwono X before the gathering dispersed.

Violence erupted later that evening when approximately 100 people gathered near the provincial legislative council building and allegedly threw stones, firecrackers and Molotov cocktails, according to police.

Security forces deployed armored vehicles, water cannons and tear gas as clashes spread through parts of the city and continued into early Wednesday.

Police initially reported 154 detentions but subsequently raised the figure to 157, including 21 minors. Investigations director Yani Permana said officers were examining the detainees’ alleged involvement in the disturbances. Police said they were coordinating with child protection officials over the handling of the 21 minors.

HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS DEMAND INQUIRY

Rights group Amnesty International Indonesia called for an independent investigation into allegations of excessive force, arbitrary detentions and the deployment of military personnel near university facilities.

The Yogyakarta Legal Aid Institute reported receiving 64 complaints by Wednesday morning. Among those cases, 47 people had reportedly been detained, 13 remained unreachable, two were hospitalized and two had returned home.

“We are very worried about reports that many are missing. Where are they? What is the army doing?” a Christian told Worthy News, expressing concern about the fate of demonstrators.

The legal aid organization’s figures represented individual complaints rather than the overall police detention total. Those described as unreachable had not necessarily been confirmed missing.

Amnesty also expressed concern about tear gas spreading toward Gadjah Mada University and Panti Rapih Hospital, saying verified footage showed gas near the hospital’s emergency department. Police denied entering the university campus, while National Police Chief General Suyudi Ario Seto promised to investigate the violence and whether unidentified groups had deliberately provoked confrontations.

POLICE ENTER CHURCHES

Additionally, police entered churches across Indonesia in recent weeks, addressing congregations during or around worship services, according to Indonesian sources and police statements.

Authorities described the visits as part of Minggu Kasih, or Sunday of Love, a nationwide outreach initiative promoted under National Police Chief Suyudi’s 2026 program.

Officers have introduced police greetings and promoted the slogan Polisi Bersama Masyarakat, meaning “Police Together With the Community.” Suyudi maintained that the initiative was intended to strengthen relations with religious communities and protect worshippers.

However, critics questioned the presence of uniformed officers inside churches amid protests against government policies. Indonesian human rights advocate Ardi Manto Adiputra, director of the organization Imparsial, warned that such visits could potentially constitute intimidation.

Some worshippers complained that police presentations disrupted religious activities. Christians in the Yogyakarta area also said officers had warned church members against participating in demonstrations, raising concerns that the outreach program could discourage peaceful political expression.

WORSHIPPERS QUESTION POLICE

On Sunday, November 8, officers visited congregations in Palembang, Ternate, Nabire, Pekanbaru, Bengkulu, Manado and Kupang, according to Indonesian media reports and police statements.

Similar visits were reported in Jakarta, parts of Kalimantan and other regions, prompting questions about the boundaries between police outreach, religious freedom and political activity.

The controversy followed sermons on November 1 in which several Protestant pastors raised three fingers, adopting a gesture associated with student demonstrations and calls for social justice.

At GPIB Marga Mulya church in Yogyakarta, Reverend Jimmy Marcos Immanuel Sormin encouraged worshippers to consider their responsibility toward people suffering from injustice and hardship. He also criticized problems surrounding the government’s free nutritious meals program, which has faced scrutiny over food poisoning incidents.

Reverend Risang Anggoro Elliarso of GKJ Condongcatur church linked the gesture to the Protestant Reformation and the importance of confronting abuses of power, while Reverend Rena Sesaria Yudhita of GKI Gejayan church urged Christians not to remain silent when justice is denied.

CHRISTIANS DEFEND RIGHT TO SPEAK

“When justice is ignored, when life is trampled upon for the interests of those in power, faith must take a stand, faith must speak, faith must demand,” Yudhita told worshippers, according to remarks translated from Indonesian.

She challenged congregants to consider whether Christians should always obey authority or sometimes demand accountability. Her church later explained that the three-finger gesture represented a call to love rather than hatred, build rather than destroy, and promote peace.

Indonesia, a sprawling Southeast Asian archipelago of roughly 280 million people, has the world’s largest Muslim population but also significant Protestant and Catholic communities. Its constitution recognizes religious freedom, although minorities have periodically faced discrimination, restrictions and intimidation.

President Prabowo, a former military general, has emphasized stability and national security while facing growing demands for economic reforms and greater accountability. Human rights organizations have warned that maintaining public order must not undermine peaceful assembly, freedom of expression or religious liberty.

For Christians speaking to Worthy News, the immediate concern is that confrontations between demonstrators and security forces could escalate. They say they are praying for peace and restraint as Indonesia faces political uncertainty following Gibran’s reported resignation.

The post Indonesia Vice President Resigns Amid Protests As Christians Report Police Intimidation In Churches (Worthy News In-Depth) appeared first on Worthy Christian News.

articles.title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
articles.content:
Stopping an AI agent is easy. The hard part is what your business runs on in the minute after.

On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.”

Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure.

The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead?

A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled

Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop.

It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works.

Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue.

That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself.

The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path.

What a fallback has to do

I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover, patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name.

Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then.

  • The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live.
  • The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them.
  • Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals.
  • The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope.

How I’d build fallback-first today

If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live.

  • A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident.
  • A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it.
  • Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns.
  • A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it.
  • Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day.

None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone.

Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull.

Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

articles.title: Worldwide Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, and more [updated]
articles.content:
This is a developing story. We’ll update this article as more information becomes available.

.kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kt-inside-inner-col > .kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > }@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column488461_efee3d-5c > }

In this article

  • What’s affected by the Microsoft 365 outage
  • What Microsoft has said about the cause and recovery efforts
  • Where to check for updates and what to keep in mind about security

A widespread Microsoft outage is disrupting Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services, including SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot. Reportedly, the problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued into Friday, affecting people trying to access email, communicate with colleagues, and use workplace applications.

Microsoft initially reported problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas, but disruption subsequently extended beyond that region. CNN reports impacts on businesses, schools, and government services, including in Australia.

There are a lot of questions we’ll try to answer as the day evolves.

What’s affected?

Outlook users have reported being unable to send or receive emails or even load their inboxes. Other affected services include SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot, although availability has varied: some people have been able to use certain applications while others remain inaccessible.

Outage tracker Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

What’s the cause?

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said there was no indication that malicious activity or a cyberattack caused the outage. The underlying cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said some servers became unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks. That left the remaining infrastructure handling extra traffic, contributing to connection problems. The underlying reason for the failures was not immediately clear.

Recovery has not been straightforward. Microsoft restored some servers, but subsequently said they could become unresponsive again when traffic returned. Other attempted changes also failed to deliver the expected improvement.

Update  November 13, 10:01 UTC (05:01 EST): Microsoft says it currently has no evidence that malicious activity caused the outage. The company says it will publish a full post-incident report once mitigation is complete, detailing the root cause and additional safeguards to help prevent similar incidents.

Final update November 13: Microsoft states: This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

How long will it take to restore services?

At the time of writing, Microsoft has not provided a timeframe for full restoration. The company reported partial recovery in some regions, after earlier attempts produced mixed results.

For updates, check Microsoft’s service status page and its Microsoft 365 Status account on X. Both are channels Microsoft is using to communicate about the incident.

Update, November 13, 09:57 UTC (04:57 EST): Microsoft says its latest traffic optimization measures are producing “positive results for service stability and increased capacity.” The company is continuing to restore affected servers and monitor recovery, but full restoration has not yet been confirmed in the updates reviewed. Earlier improvements proved temporary, with Microsoft reporting partial recovery that was not sustained.

Update, November 13, 12:11 UTC (07:11 EST): Microsoft says it has made further progress toward recovery, with traffic gradually being restored across portions of the affected infrastructure. The company is seeing improvements in mailbox access and delayed-email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent problems. Recovery work is continuing across the remaining affected infrastructure. Microsoft has also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect delayed messages while recovery continues. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Update, November 13, 13:46 UTC (08:46 EST): Microsoft says recovery is progressing across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. The company is also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Some users may still experience intermittent access problems or delayed email delivery as recovery work continues across the remaining affected infrastructure. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Final update November 13: Microsoft says: We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

What about security?

ABC reports that Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 are both on Microsoft’s list of services that may be affected.

Being unable to log in doesn’t mean attackers are also locked out, or that every security feature has stopped working. If you rely on these services, check which security features are working as access is restored. Follow your IT team’s guidance and check Microsoft’s updates for details.

Be alert for unexpected messages offering to restore access or asking you to sign in through a link. Go directly to Microsoft’s official status pages instead.

Malwarebytes and ThreatDown products are not affected by this outage.

articles.title: Malaysia turns to Türkiye for naval strike missiles
articles.content:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia has picked Türkiye as its preferred supplier of an alternative missile system for the navy’s Littoral Combat Ships (LCS) after Norway failed to issue the export licence needed for the naval strike missiles (NSM).

Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the government would begin negotiations with Türkiye to finalise the proposed replacement after evaluating alternatives from three countries.

He said Türkiye was selected based on several factors, including price, delivery timelines and initial costs.

“The countries we invited to submit proposals were Türkiye, France and Italy. Following our evaluation, we identified Türkiye as the best option to replace the NSM missiles from Norway.

“We will now engage with the Turkish side for further negotiations before making a final decision,” he told reporters after the ministry’s 2026 Innovation Day celebration on Thursday (Nov 12).

Mohamed Khaled said Malaysia had accepted that it would not receive the NSM missiles despite having made payments and fulfilled its obligations under the procurement agreement because the Norwegian government had not issued the necessary export licence.

He said the government was now pursuing the contractual dispute resolution process, which involves several stages before the matter can proceed to arbitration.

“The first stage, involving amicable negotiations between both parties, has been completed without a resolution.

“Malaysia will now proceed with the establishment of a dispute resolution committee,” he said.

If the second stage also fails to resolve the dispute, Malaysia will proceed to arbitration, which can be held in Kuala Lumpur under the terms of the contract, he added.

“However, all these processes will take time, and we cannot predict when the matter will be resolved or when the Norwegian company will refund the money,” he said.

Mohamed Khaled stressed that Malaysia would not wait for the refund before securing an alternative missile system for its naval vessels.

He said the proposed Turkish system appeared compatible with the LCS and capable of being integrated with the vessels, although these aspects would be examined further during negotiations.

He also said the replacement would not require Malaysia to procure an entirely new stock of missiles because the same missile system had already been ordered for the navy’s Littoral Mission Ships (LMS).

“This would allow Malaysia to obtain an initial supply earlier, potentially by 2028, instead of waiting until 2029 if a fresh order had to be placed,” he said.

Mohamed Khaled said the missile had a surface-to-surface range of 250km and was considered competitive in terms of its capabilities.

He said Malaysia would mainly incur additional costs for launchers and integration work rather than having to purchase an entirely new stock of missiles.

“If we had to order new missiles from scratch, the cost could be between US$700mil and US$900mil.

“We do not need to spend that amount now because the missiles have already been ordered for the LMS,” he said.

Mohamed Khaled said the negotiations would be conducted through a government-to-government arrangement involving the relevant Turkish government agency rather than directly with a private company.

articles.title: Vietnamese, Lao provinces work to protect shared border
articles.content:
QUANG TRI – Leaders of Việt Nam’s Quảng Trị Province and Laos’s Savannakhet province agreed to strengthen border security, step up joint patrols and promote cross-border trade at their meeting following a bilateral border patrol and inspection on Thursday.

The activity was attended by Secretary of the Quảng Trị provincial Party Committee Vương Quốc Tuấn and Secretary of the Party Committee and Chairman of the provincial People’s Council of Savannakhet province Bounchom Ubonpaseuth, along with officials and border forces from both sides.

The patrol covered border markers 604, 605 and 606, the Lao Bảo–Den Savanh international border gate and a section of the Sê Pôn River from Border Post 18 to Border Post 25. The two sides inspected border markers, assessed security conditions and discussed coordination in border management.

The inspection found that all border markers remained intact and the security situation in the area was stable. Both sides also identified potential risks, including smuggling, illegal immigration and other cross-border violations.

At a subsequent meeting, leaders of the two provinces agreed to strengthen information sharing, maintain regular joint patrols and improve coordination in preventing cross-border crimes and managing the movement of residents across the border.

They also discussed upgrading border gate infrastructure, developing the Lao Bảo–Den Savanh cross-border economic and trade zone, and applying digital technologies to build smart border gates and facilitate legitimate trade.

Tuấn stressed that economic development must go hand in hand with national defence and security and the maintenance of a peaceful, friendly and cooperative border.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to implementing Việt Nam–Laos border agreements, raising public awareness of border regulations and working together to maintain stability and promote sustainable development in border areas.

The joint patrol and meeting are expected to strengthen coordination between the two provinces and contribute to the special solidarity and comprehensive cooperation between Việt Nam and Laos.

articles.title: Thai navy searches for six crew members after tanker sinks off Chonburi
articles.content:
BANGKOK – The Royal Thai Navy’s First Naval Area Command launched an urgent search and rescue operation for six crew members on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), after receiving a report that the Venus 14, a tanker supplying fuel for fishing operations, had sunk at 9am.

The reported position was 27 miles from the entrance to the Sattahip Naval Base navigation channel, on a bearing of 227 degrees.

The command immediately dispatched patrol boat T.113 and a Do 228 patrol aircraft for the search and rescue operation.

It was also checking for oil leakage and verifying the location of the sunken vessel, while alerting passing vessels to ensure navigational safety.

The command also coordinated with the Marine Department to prepare for possible oil pollution.

It ordered preparations for the naval tug Panyi and a helicopter, with personnel and oil clean-up equipment to be made ready for immediate deployment upon request.

The navy confirmed its readiness to make every effort to find and rescue those in distress, while closely monitoring and working to prevent impacts on the marine environment.

articles.title: No agreement yet on second ASEAN-GCC-China Summit, says Malaysia’s Deputy Foreign Minister
articles.content:
KUALA LUMPUR – A second Asean-GCC-China Summit has yet to be agreed upon, with Malaysia remaining open to further cooperation through existing regional platforms, says Deputy Foreign Minister Datuk Lukanisman Awang Sauni.

He said the inaugural summit, hosted by Malaysia in May 2025, was agreed upon as a one-off event by all Asean member states.

“Discussions and meetings have yet to reach a common understanding on organising another Asean-GCC-China Summit,” he said during question time in the Dewan Rakyat on Thursday (Nov 12).

However, Lukanisman said Malaysia would continue strengthening ties through existing mechanisms, including Asean-China and Asean-GCC cooperation.

He was responding to Tan Kok Wai (PH-Cheras), who asked about follow-up measures to implement the joint statement adopted at the 2025 summit and when the next meeting would be held.

The joint statement outlined cooperation in trade and investment, energy, technology, connectivity, and inclusive and sustainable growth.

“The partnership can also help strengthen regional energy supply chains amid the conflict in West Asia, which has placed pressure on global energy security,” he said.

He added that Malaysia hoped future Asean chairmanships would follow its lead in organising initiatives to strengthen Asean-GCC-China cooperation.

In a supplementary question, Tan asked whether the partnership could be expanded into a broader Asian summit involving countries from South Asia, East Asia and Central Asia.

Lukanisman said Malaysia would continue exploring opportunities to strengthen economic ties through existing platforms, while remaining open to broader cooperation.

Separately, responding to Dr Halimah Ali (PN-Kapar), he said the Foreign Ministry had included halal diplomacy in its briefing notes for Malaysian diplomats to promote the country’s halal industry as part of its economic diplomacy efforts.

Halimah had proposed establishing an Asean-GCC-China Business Council to connect businesses, chambers of commerce and investors across the three regions, particularly to help Malaysian small and medium enterprises and halal businesses access wider markets.

Lukanisman said the proposal was still under discussion and could be raised with the relevant ministries if another summit was held.

articles.title: Human Rights Watch urges ASEAN to step up pressure on Myanmar junta
articles.content:
MANILA – Human Rights Watch (HRW) on Thursday urged Southeast Asian leaders gathering in the Philippines this weekend to increase pressure on Myanmar’s military junta to end attacks on civilians, lift restrictions on humanitarian assistance and begin credible dialogue on a transition to civilian rule.

In a Nov. 5 letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the Philippines’ president and 2026 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) chair, HRW also called on the regional bloc to maintain its refusal to recognize or endorse what it described as sham elections earlier this year that resulted in junta leader Min Aung Hlaing assuming Myanmar’s presidency.

The Philippine government confirmed on Nov. 11 that Min Aung Hlaing would not attend the Nov. 15 to 17 Asean and related summits.

However, HRW noted that several governments in Asean and the region had hosted the junta leader in recent months despite his administration’s rejection of the bloc’s calls to address Myanmar’s human rights and humanitarian crisis.

The upcoming meetings will bring together Asean leaders and their counterparts from partner countries and organizations, including the United States, European Union, Japan, China and India.

“Asean could play an important role in bringing a stop to Myanmar military abuses,” said John Sifton, Asia advocacy director at Human Rights Watch.

“Governments should be increasing pressure on the junta to end its attacks on civilians, lift restrictions on humanitarian aid, and begin credible dialogues about transitioning to civilian rule,” he added.

As commander in chief of Myanmar’s military before and after the 2021 military coup, Min Aung Hlaing has led numerous military operations across the country that HRW said involved abuses, many of which included war crimes and crimes against humanity.

According to the human rights watchdog, junta authorities have arrested more than 32,000 people for opposing military rule, with at least 2,300 reportedly dying in custody. HRW added that detainees have also faced torture and ill-treatment.

“Over 6,600 of those arrested have been women, and Human Rights Watch recently documented that many of them have experienced sexual violence as well as dangerous and sometimes deadly denials of prenatal and obstetric medical care,” HRW said in a statement.

In its Nov. 5 letter to Marcos, the group stressed that more than 4 million people have also been internally displaced in Myanmar.

Many have sought shelter in makeshift camps, forests and open fields, with limited access to food, clean water and health care.

“Skyrocketing prices, foreign aid cuts, and restrictions on medical care and humanitarian supplies have exacerbated malnutrition, waterborne illness, and preventable deaths,” it added.

Calls for humanitarian aid, refugee protection

HRW urged Asean members to use the upcoming meetings to strengthen humanitarian assistance and protect Myanmar nationals who have fled to neighboring countries.

In its letter to Marcos, the group outlined specific measures Asean could take to improve humanitarian access and protect Myanmar nationals who have fled to neighboring countries.

“Asean should press the junta not to impede access to aid for groups at risk. Myanmar is obligated under international humanitarian law to not withhold consent for relief operations on arbitrary grounds,” HRW said.

It also called on Asean members to channel their own humanitarian assistance through independent local organizations “rather than only through junta authorities.”

HRW said local groups have the networks and experience needed to navigate difficult conditions and reach communities most in need.

The group also cited concerns over the military’s record of corruption and misuse of disaster assistance funds and supplies.

On refugee protection, HRW said conditions for safe, dignified and voluntary return to Myanmar do not currently exist for those who have fled the country.

“Asean members and other countries should affirm not to forcibly return refugees to Myanmar. They should explore ways of allowing refugees to regularize their status, including through the granting of work rights,” the group said.

“Refugees should be allowed to seek work opportunities to help support themselves and their families,” it added.

HRW stressed that Asean members should comply with targeted sanctions imposed by international partners, including the European Union, United Kingdom and United States, against junta officials and military-controlled companies.

These measures include freezing assets and blocking transactions involving sanctioned entities in Myanmar and other Asean jurisdictions.

Calls for accountability

HRW also urged Asean to support international efforts to hold the Myanmar military accountable for alleged atrocities, citing decades of impunity and insufficient action to address abuses.

In its letter to Marcos, the rights group said:

“The Myanmar junta’s continuing war crimes and crimes against humanity have been fueled by decades of impunity and insufficient global efforts to end its violations and hold perpetrators to account. Asean should support the work of international accountability mechanisms, and its members should be ready to take necessary steps to facilitate the implementation of the upcoming ICJ judgment.”

The group also called on Cambodia and Timor-Leste, both parties to the Rome Statute, to fulfill their obligations to execute ICC arrest warrants, regardless of whom they target. It urged the Philippines to rejoin the international court.

The letter further addressed legal proceedings against the Myanmar military being considered by domestic courts under the principle of universal jurisdiction.

“Asean members whose courts are considering legal cases against the Myanmar military under the principle of universal jurisdiction—Indonesia, the Philippines, and Timor-Leste—should allow judicial authorities to make their determinations free from any political interference.”

International court proceedings

The regional meetings will take place days before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, Netherlands, is scheduled to deliver its judgment on Nov. 19 in the landmark case brought by Gambia against Myanmar over alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

The case concerns allegations that Myanmar’s 2017 military campaign against the ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State violated the Genocide Convention.

HRW said Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the campaign, which involved massacres, rape and arson.

The ICJ proceedings concern Myanmar’s responsibility as a state under the Genocide Convention rather than criminal charges against Min Aung Hlaing personally.

Min Aung Hlaing is also under investigation by the ICC over alleged atrocities committed against the Rohingya.

In November 2024, the court’s prosecutor sought an arrest warrant against him, alleging his involvement in the deportation and persecution of the ethnic group as crimes against humanity during the military’s 2017 campaign.

The judges have not publicly ruled on the application, HRW said.

“Concerned governments need to undertake tougher measures to pressure and compel Myanmar’s junta to stop committing abuses and engage in real dialogue,” Sifton said.

articles.title: Brianna Ross: Grief, unanswered questions, and a fight for change
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | iHeartRadio | Podcast Index | RSS

Jason Christopher Ross served his country as a Marine corporal in Iraq. At home, he was a husband and father who loved the life he and his wife, Brianna, had built with their three children.

He was 36 when he died on October 25, 2021, after roughly 18 days in a hospital with COVID-19.

For Brianna Ross, the loss became a call to protect other families. She believes hospital treatment and the dismissal of her concerns cost Jason his life. Her account carries a demand that should matter to every American: Patients and families deserve a voice when medical decisions carry irreversible consequences.

Ross describes being separated from her husband, struggling to reach caregivers, and having requests for different treatments rejected. She says efforts to bring him home failed. A hospital should never leave a family feeling powerless, frightened, and unheard.

Her advocacy reaches beyond one hospital stay. She wants independent patient advocates who answer to families, meaningful informed consent, and a path to accountability when care goes wrong.

She sees federal liability protections under the PREP Act as a major barrier to pursuing her claims. Her frustration is sharpened by the years that have passed without the accountability she seeks.

That frustration has not extinguished her hope in Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or the Make America Healthy Again movement. Ross wants faster progress, yet recognizes that changing entrenched systems means navigating political resistance. She supports removing harmful substances from food and shifting incentives toward better health.

The work ahead must include families still carrying the weight of pandemic losses. Ross hopes for further congressional attention, legislative action, and support for surviving spouses and children.

Her message is rooted in grief, but directed toward prevention. Remember the families. Hear their accounts. Give them a fair chance to seek answers and meaningful accountability.

articles.title: Palo Alto tracks a massive Chinese AI attack that sadly lives up to industry fears
articles.content:
Vastly different attack vectors were used as the AI tailored its campaign to each target.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said.

The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems.

It even gained unauthenticated access to cloud storage and overwrote a live ballot for a vote on an industry standard. Through separate flaws, the attackers logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions.

“What a nightmare,” said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “This campaign is impressive, in the worst way.”

He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval.

Unit 42 “took the machine apart and showed how it thinks: the shared blackboard, the facts, the intents, the human hints, and even the exact prompts the attackers used,” he said. “The expensive part of an intrusion was always the labor: the reconnaissance, the trial and error, and the patience. That labor is now a line item on an API bill. Unit 42 believes one person or a handful of people ran all of it, hitting 19 organizations in two weeks. Some operations ran for more than 50 hours.”

Andy Piazza, senior director of threat research at Unit 42, said the monitored campaign showed that the massive scope of a global AI-fueled assault is every bit as frightening as predicted.

“We are now starting to see the evidence” because the monitored campaign “can now interact with 1,000 organizations at the same time,” Piazza said. “I think we need to throw out the risk model for the perimeter. This also completely breaks our attribution models. The fingerprinting of attack uniqueness is going to be a hell of a lot harder now.”

Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that he was concerned about this campaign because of the scope of activities that AI is now able to handle.

“This is significant because AI is taking on the coordination of an intrusion, using each result to decide what to try next and reducing the hands-on effort required to pursue multiple targets,” he said. “That changes the economics of targeting. An attacker can sustain pressure across more organizations without personally directing every step. An organization’s risk can rise even when its vulnerabilities haven’t changed.”

Greis noted that the altered ballot deserves attention because it shows how an intrusion can undermine the information people rely on to make decisions. “Alongside detecting data theft, CISOs should monitor unauthorized changes to critical records and privileged access and test their ability to verify and restore trusted information after an incident,” he said. “Resilience includes knowing that the information you are using to run the business can still be trusted.”

The model’s process

The report included a detailed description of the campaign’s methodology. “Cairn coordinated its activities through a shared blackboard,” it said. “Agents read the blackboard and wrote their ﬁndings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject hints at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Conﬁrmed ﬁndings accumulate as immutable facts and the agent queues its next actions as intents. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the US.”

The model produced a different plan for each target, each running between three and seven stages, the researchers explained. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Chinese AI Models Cairn is model-agnostic, they noted, and the attackers ran their operations on the Chinese models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro.

The report also described attackers’ efforts to negate systems attempting to prohibit the unauthorized activities.

“Cairn’s stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task,” it said. “The attackers reinforced this with an authorization pretext of their own. Each operation also generated an authorization.md file. This file declared the operation authorized, treating the attackers’ act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement. The attackers seeded each task with an organization’s root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface.”

“We knew attackers would get here. We hoped it was not now,” Dickson said. “AI attack agents have graduated from failed experiments to real breaches, and they did it in about three months.”

articles.title: LEGO’s BrickLink taken offline: What users should know
articles.content:

In this article

  • LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting unusual activity
  • The company has not confirmed a hack or whether customer data was affected
  • Users should watch for suspicious payment requests and avoid reusing passwords

LEGO collectors looking for a missing piece have a bigger problem to contend with: accessing the specialized marketplace BrickLink.

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting what it calls “unusual activity.” The company says it is investigating before bringing the marketplace back, but has not disclosed whether attackers accessed its systems or whether customer information was affected.

BrickLink allows users to buy and sell LEGO parts, sets, and minifigures, making it a useful resource for collectors and a business platform for independent sellers. LEGO acquired the fan-founded marketplace in 2019. Its disruption leaves more than unfinished builds on hold: sellers also depend on access to orders and their storefronts.

The BrickLink website previously said it would remain unavailable until at least Wednesday, November 11. That date has now been removed, with no replacement given.

We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform. Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

This work is still on-going and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible.

Updated: 11th November 2026

According to the BBC, LEGO had not provided details confirming a hack or explaining whether customer data was affected.

Specialist LEGO publications reported that BrickLink went offline around November 5. An article published the following morning described a notice saying the site was unavailable while teams carried out “necessary work.” That report also noted that users could not access storefronts, profiles, order histories, or the Designer Program page.

In November 2023, BrickLink also closed down after it noticed what turned out to be credential stuffing attacks.

The BBC also reported the experience of a BrickLink customer who received repeated payment links for a limited-edition preorder she said she had already paid for. The dispute was subsequently resolved, and LEGO told the BBC it was not aware of wider payment issues. But there is no established connection between that payment problem and the activity that prompted the shutdown.

How to stay safe

Until we know what the issue is, it is hard to provide targeted advice, but users can take a few proportionate precautions:

  • Watch for unexpected account or payment messages. A request to “restore access,” confirm payment information, or resolve an urgent account problem deserves scrutiny, because these are common phishing themes.
  • Verify requests through an independent route. Use the official website or an established support channel rather than following links in an unexpected email or text.
  • Use unique passwords. If your BrickLink password is also used elsewhere, change it on those other services now. Use a password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords. Change your BrickLink password once the site is available again.

BrickLink’s shutdown is disruptive, but the available evidence does not yet justify calling it a confirmed data breach. For now, the priority for users is to follow official updates, check unexpected payment requests carefully, and watch for scams exploiting the outage.
